Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 89, verses 1–4:

﴿By the dawn﴾ ﴿and by ten nights﴾ ﴿and by the even and the odd﴾ ﴿and by the night when it passes﴾.

The oath by these times is because some of them are indications of the marvellous creation of God and the vastness of His power in the order He established, in which some parts manifest others. Among these is the time of dawn (fajr), which combines the end of the darkness of night with the beginning of the light of day, and the time of night in which darkness reaches its fullness. These are, in addition, times for acts of righteousness and the worship of God alone, such as the ten nights, the even nights and the odd nights.

The purpose of this oath is to affirm the thing sworn to, because the oath in speech is one of the means of emphasising a statement, since an oath is calling on one's Lord to witness what one's speech contains.

The oath of God, exalted is He, is purely for the purpose of emphasis.

The address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad?﴾ [al-Fajr 89:6] and His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is in ambush.﴾ [al-Fajr 89:14].

Therefore the oath implies an affirmation that what is sworn to will occur, with respect to the deniers.

The purpose of lengthening the oath by mentioning several things is to create eagerness for the thing sworn to.

Al-Fajr (dawn) is the name for the time when light begins to appear at the farthest east, from the first rays of the sun, when darkness recedes from the first line that becomes visible to the observer among the hypothetical lines known in the drawing of the terrestrial globe in geography. Then it extends and lights the horizon, then the sun appears at sunrise. It is a great manifestation of divine power and marvellous creation.

Thus al-Fajr is the beginning of the appearance of light after the darkness of night has begun to break up. It is a blessed time for people, for at it the state that calls to sleep, which is like death, comes to an end, and people begin to regain their senses and turn to the beneficial works to which they are accustomed.

The definite article in (al-Fajr) is the definite article of the genus, and this is the more apparent meaning, in view of the conjunction with (﴿and by the night when it passes﴾).

It is also possible that a specific dawn is meant. It has been said that the time of the dawn prayer every day is meant, and this is from Qatadah. It has also been said that it is the dawn of the day of sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), which is the dawn in which the pilgrims are at Muzdalifah, and this is from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah. In that case the definite article of (al-Fajr) is the definite article of prior reference.

As for His saying: (﴿and by ten nights﴾): these are nights known to the listeners, described as being ten, and their definition is dispensed with by describing them as ten. Since you have described the number with them, it is determined that they are ten consecutive nights. The definite article was dropped although they are known, so that by omitting the definite article one may arrive at their tanwin (nunation), which conveys magnification. There are no ten consecutive nights in the nights of the year as great as the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, which is the time of the rites of the Hajj. In them occur the ihram, entering Makkah, and the acts of tawaf. On its eighth night is the Night of Tarwiyah, its ninth is the Night of 'Arafah, and its tenth is the Night of Sacrifice. It is therefore determined that these are the nights intended by "ten nights". This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr. Ahmad and al-Nasa'i related from Abu al-Zubayr (al-Makki) from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Indeed the ten are the ten of al-Adha (the sacrifice)." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "It is not authentically established." Ibn 'Asakir said: "Its narrators are not objectionable, but in my view the text, in its being traced back to the Prophet, contains a denounced irregularity (nakarah)." End of quote.

The reason for conjoining "ten nights" to "dawn" is that dawn is the time of the end of the night, so between it and the night there is the bond of opposition. The night is a manifestation of divine power. When it was intended to conjoin it to dawn with His saying (﴿and by the night when it passes﴾), the blessed nights were specified by mention before it, since they are among the individual instances of the night.

The ten nights were specified by God, exalted is He, in the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Then their timings were changed by what the people of the Jahiliyyah introduced into the lunar year of intercalation (al-nasi'), so the sacred years that God had commanded to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, became disordered. It is not known when that disorder began, nor the quantities of the intercalation introduced into them, nor what fixes the days of intercalation in each year, because of the differences in their conventions and the absence of any fixed rule. Therefore it is impossible to determine the ten nights commanded by God, exalted is He. Nevertheless we are certain of their existence through the course of the year, until God revealed to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in the tenth year of the Hijrah, the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, that the months of Hajj in that year coincided with what the year had been in the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. So the Prophet ﷺ said in his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed time has turned back to its form on the day God created the heavens and the earth."

This change does not remove the blessing of the days in which the rites took place before the Farewell Pilgrimage, because God magnified them on account of what takes place in them of the rites of the Hajj, since it is worship purely to God.

The times of acts of worship are determinations for performing the worship, so there is no doubt that for the fixed time of their performance there is a wisdom known to God, exalted is He. For this reason it became prevalent in the expressions of the jurists and the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh) to apply the term "cause" (sabab) to the time, since by "cause" they mean that which is defined by the ruling, and they do not mean by it the wisdom itself.

The determination of times for acts of worship is among the matters in which God alone is unique. Therefore the times of acts of worship have sanctity by divine ordainment. But when they differ or become mixed, their disruption or confusion does not require the cancellation of the acts of worship specified for them.

Thus God's oath by the ten nights in this verse, and it is among what was revealed in Makkah, is an oath by what is in His knowledge of their determination.

Al-shaf' (the even) is that which is second to another, and al-watr (the odd) is the single thing. These two are adjectives of an omitted noun. On the authority of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet ﷺ, the even is the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). That is because it is the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the relevance of beginning with the even is that it is the tenth day, which suits His saying (﴿ten nights﴾). And the odd is the Day of 'Arafah, related by Ahmad ibn Hanbal and al-Nasa'i, as previously mentioned. According to this interpretation, the mention of the even and the odd singles out these two days for mention for emphasis, after the ten nights have included them both.

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of 'Imran ibn Husayn, the Prophet ﷺ said: "The even and the odd: the prayer, of which some is even and some is odd." al-Tirmidhi said: "It is a gharib hadith." In al-'Aridah it is stated that its chain contains an unknown narrator. Ibn Kathir said: "In my view its attribution as a statement of 'Imran ibn Husayn is more likely."

It is appropriate to interpret the verse according to both interpretations.

It has also been said that the even is the two days after the day of Mina, and the odd is the third day, and these are the numbered days (al-ayyam al-ma'dudat), so they would be other than the ten nights.

The indefiniteness of "nights" (layalin) and the definiteness of "the even and the odd" indicate that the ten nights are specific nights, which are ten nights every year. The definiteness of "the even and the odd" indicates that they are known, and that they are the even and the odd among the ten nights.

Regarding the interpretation of the even and the odd there are eighteen sayings, some of which overlap. al-Qurtubi compiled them, and most of them do not fit well as the meaning of the verse, since there is no relevance in them for the conjunction with "ten nights".

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read (wa-l-watri) with a fatha on the waw, and this is the dialect of Quraysh and the people of the Hijaz. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the waw, and this is the dialect of Tamim and Bakr ibn Sa'd ibn Bakr, who are the Banu Sa'd, the foster-kin of the Prophet ﷺ, and they are the people of al-'Aliyah. So these are two dialects for al-watr, with the meaning of the single.

(Wa-l-layli) is conjoined to "ten nights", a conjunction of the more general to the more specific, or it is conjoined to "dawn" on the basis of the commonality of opposition. He swore by it because it is a manifestation of the power of God and of His marvellous wisdom.

The meaning of yasri is: it goes on travelling in the darkness; that is, when a great part of it has passed. The passing of the night in its darkness is likened to the journey of the traveller in the dark, which is al-sura, just as it is likened in His saying: ﴿and by the night when it turns back﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:33], and He said: ﴿and by the night when it becomes still﴾ [al-Duha 93:2], that is, when its darkness has settled and intensified.

The restriction of the night by the temporal clause "when it passes" is because it is the time when the darkness of the night is fully established, and at that time people have taken their share of sleep and are able to perform tahajjud (night prayer). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night is more effective in impression and more upright in speech﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:6], and He said: ﴿And from the night, prostrate to Him and glorify Him﴾ [al-Insan 76:26].

Abu Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read (idha yasri) with a ya' after the ra' in pause (wasl), following the original form, and without it in stopping (waqf), in order to observe the consistency of the verse-endings: al-fajr, 'ashr, al-watr, hijr. The verse-endings of the Qur'an are like rhymed prose (saj') in prose, and rhymed prose is treated like the rhyme of poetry. Abu 'Ali said: "Retaining the ya' in pause is not better than omitting it." All words that are not normally omitted, and for which omission is preferred when they are in a rhyme or verse-ending, such as al-qadi with the definite article, are omitted when they are in a rhyme or verse-ending; but if they are not a verse-ending, then retaining the ya' is preferable. Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read with the ya' retained after the ra' both in connection and in stopping, following the original form. The rest read without the ya', both in connection and in stopping. This transmission is supported by the orthography of the Mushaf, which is without the ya'. Those who retained the ya' in both connection and stopping relied on the transmission, and regarded the orthography of the Mushaf as a sunnah, or as taking into account that the writing is according to the state of stopping.

As for Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far, the orthography of the Mushaf does not weaken their transmission, because the orthography of the Mushaf came in consideration of the state of stopping, and consideration of stopping is frequent in the modes of orthography.

That is because it is the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, and the relevance of beginning with the even is that it is the tenth day, which suits His saying (﴿ten nights﴾). In al-'Aridah it is stated that its chain contains an unknown narrator. Ibn Kathir said: "In my view its attribution as a statement of 'Imran ibn Husayn is more likely."

It is appropriate to interpret the verse according to both interpretations.

It has also been said that the even is the two days after the day of Mina, and the odd is the third day, and these are the numbered days (al-ayyam al-ma'dudat), so they would be other than the ten nights.

The definiteness of "the even and the odd" indicates that they are known, and that they are the even and the odd among the ten nights.

Regarding the interpretation of the even and the odd there are eighteen sayings, some of which overlap. al-Qurtubi compiled them, and most of them do not fit well as the meaning of the verse, since there is no relevance in them for the conjunction with "ten nights".

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read (wa-l-watri) with a fatha on the waw, and this is the dialect of Quraysh and the people of the Hijaz. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the waw, and this is the dialect of Tamim and Bakr ibn Sa'd ibn Bakr, who are the Banu Sa'd, the foster-kin of the Prophet ﷺ, and they are the people of al-'Aliyah. So these are two dialects for al-watr, with the meaning of the single.

(Wa-l-layli) is conjoined to "ten nights", a conjunction of the more general to the more specific, or it is conjoined to "dawn" on the basis of the commonality of opposition. He swore by it because it is a manifestation of the power of God and of His marvellous wisdom.

The meaning of yasri is: it goes on travelling in the darkness; that is, when a great part of it has passed. The passing of the night in its darkness is likened to the journey of the traveller in the dark, which is al-sura, just as it is likened in His saying: ﴿and by the night when it turns back﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:33], and He said: ﴿and by the night when it becomes still﴾ [al-Duha 93:2], that is, when its darkness has settled and intensified.

The restriction of the night by the temporal clause "when it passes" is because it is the time when the darkness of the night is fully established, and at that time people have taken their share of sleep and are able to perform tahajjud (night prayer). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night is more effective in impression and more upright in speech﴾ [al-Muzzammil 73:6], and He said: ﴿And from the night, prostrate to Him and glorify Him﴾ [al-Insan 76:26].

The verse-endings of the Qur'an are like rhymed prose (saj') in prose, and rhymed prose is treated like the rhyme of poetry. Abu 'Ali said: "Retaining the ya' in pause is not better than omitting it." All words that are not normally omitted, and for which omission is preferred when they are in a rhyme or verse-ending, such as al-qadi with the definite article, are omitted when they are in a rhyme or verse-ending; but if they are not a verse-ending, then retaining the ya' is preferable. As for Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far, the orthography of the Mushaf does not weaken their transmission, because the orthography of the Mushaf came in consideration of the state of stopping, and consideration of stopping is frequent in the modes of orthography.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 89, verses 1–4:

﴿By the dawn﴾ ﴿and by ten nights﴾ ﴿and by the even and the odd﴾ ﴿and by the night when it passes﴾.

The oath by these times is because some of them are indications of the marvellous creation of God and the vastness of His power in the order He established, in which some parts manifest others. Among these is the time of dawn (fajr), which combines the end of the darkness of night with the beginning of the light of day, and the time of night in which darkness reaches its fullness. These are, in addition, times for acts of righteousness and the worship of God alone, such as the ten nights, the even nights and the odd nights.

The purpose of this oath is to affirm the thing sworn to, because the oath in speech is one of the means of emphasising a statement, since an oath is calling on one's Lord to witness what one's speech contains.

The oath of God, exalted is He, is purely for the purpose of emphasis.

The address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad?﴾ [al-Fajr 89:6] and His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is in ambush.﴾ [al-Fajr 89:14].

Therefore the oath implies an affirmation that what is sworn to will occur, with respect to the deniers.

The purpose of lengthening the oath by mentioning several things is to create eagerness for the thing sworn to.

Al-Fajr (dawn) is the name for the time when light begins to appear at the farthest east, from the first rays of the sun, when darkness recedes from the first line that becomes visible to the observer among the hypothetical lines known in the drawing of the terrestrial globe in geography. Then it extends and lights the horizon, then the sun appears at sunrise. It is a great manifestation of divine power and marvellous creation.

Thus al-Fajr is the beginning of the appearance of light after the darkness of night has begun to break up. It is a blessed time for people, for at it the state that calls to sleep, which is like death, comes to an end, and people begin to regain their senses and turn to the beneficial works to which they are accustomed.

The definite article in (al-Fajr) is the definite article of the genus, and this is the more apparent meaning, in view of the conjunction with (﴿and by the night when it passes﴾).

It is also possible that a specific dawn is meant. It has been said that the time of the dawn prayer every day is meant, and this is from Qatadah. It has also been said that it is the dawn of the day of sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), which is the dawn in which the pilgrims are at Muzdalifah, and this is from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah. In that case the definite article of (al-Fajr) is the definite article of prior reference.

As for His saying: (﴿and by ten nights﴾): these are nights known to the listeners, described as being ten, and their definition is dispensed with by describing them as ten. Since you have described the number with them, it is determined that they are ten consecutive nights. The definite article was dropped although they are known, so that by omitting the definite article one may arrive at their tanwin (nunation), which conveys magnification. There are no ten consecutive nights in the nights of the year as great as the ten of Dhu al-Hijjah, which is the time of the rites of the Hajj. In them occur the ihram, entering Makkah, and the acts of tawaf. On its eighth night is the Night of Tarwiyah, its ninth is the Night of 'Arafah, and its tenth is the Night of Sacrifice. It is therefore determined that these are the nights intended by "ten nights". This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr. Ahmad and al-Nasa'i related from Abu al-Zubayr (al-Makki) from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Indeed the ten are the ten of al-Adha (the sacrifice)." Ibn al-'Arabi said: "It is not authentically established." Ibn 'Asakir said: "Its narrators are not objectionable, but in my view the text, in its being traced back to the Prophet, contains a denounced irregularity (nakarah)." End of quote.

The reason for conjoining "ten nights" to "dawn" is that dawn is the time of the end of the night, so between it and the night there is the bond of opposition. The night is a manifestation of divine power. When it was intended to conjoin it to dawn with His saying (﴿and by the night when it passes﴾), the blessed nights were specified by mention before it, since they are among the individual instances of the night.

The ten nights were specified by God, exalted is He, in the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Then their timings were changed by what the people of the Jahiliyyah introduced into the lunar year of intercalation (al-nasi'), so the sacred years that God had commanded to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, became disordered. It is not known when that disorder began, nor the quantities of the intercalation introduced into them, nor what fixes the days of intercalation in each year, because of the differences in their conventions and the absence of any fixed rule. Therefore it is impossible to determine the ten nights commanded by God, exalted is He. Nevertheless we are certain of their existence through the course of the year, until God revealed to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in the tenth year of the Hijrah, the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage, that the months of Hajj in that year coincided with what the year had been in the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. So the Prophet ﷺ said in his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed time has turned back to its form on the day God created the heavens and the earth."

This change does not remove the blessing of the days in which the rites took place before the Farewell Pilgrimage, because God magnified them on account of what takes place in them of the rites of the Hajj, since it is worship purely to God.

The times of acts of worship are determinations for performing the worship, so there is no doubt that for the fixed time of their performance there is a wisdom known to God, exalted is He. This is a parenthetical clause between the oath and what follows of its answer, or of the evidence for its answer, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 76].

The interrogative is *taqriri* (a question that affirms what it asks about), and it uses the particle *hal* ("is there?") because the original function of *hal* is to indicate confirmation, since it carries the meaning of *qad* (indeed).

The demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") refers to what was sworn by. The meaning is: is there, in that oath, an oath?

The indefinite *qasam* ("an oath") is for magnification: an oath that is sufficient and convincing to the one being addressed, if he is a person of reason who reflects with his intellect.

So the meaning is: is there in that a confirmation of what He swore to, for the listener who is described as possessing *hijr*?

*Hijr* means intellect, because it restrains (*yahjuru*) its possessor from committing what is not proper, just as it is called *'aql* (from the same root as "to tie"), because it binds (*ya'qilu*) its possessor from stumbling, as the *'iqal* (hobble) binds the camel from straying.

Page 317

The *lam* in His saying *li-dhi hijr* ("for one of understanding") is the *lam* of causation, meaning: an oath for the sake of one who has intellect that prevents him from obstinacy, so that he knows that the one swearing by this oath is truthful in what he swore to.

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd,﴾ ﴿Iram of the pillars,﴾ ﴿the like of which was not created in the lands,﴾ ﴿and Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley,﴾ ﴿and Pharaoh, master of the stakes,﴾ ﴿who transgressed in the lands﴾ ﴿and increased corruption therein?﴾ ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation.﴾

This cannot serve as the answer to the oath. Rather, it is either (1) an indication of the answer (dalil al-jawab), since it shows that what is sworn to is of the same kind as what was done to these three nations, namely the total annihilation (al-isti'sal) indicated by His saying: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. The estimated answer is then: "Your Lord will surely pour upon those who deny you a scourge of punishment, just as He poured it upon ʿĀd, Thamud and Pharaoh."

Or (2) it is a preface and introduction to the answer, if you take the answer to be His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾, and what lies between it and the preceding verses is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) placed as an introduction to the answer of the oath.

The meaning is: your Lord is in observation of the deniers; nothing of their affairs is hidden from Him. This is a strengthening of the Prophet (ﷺ), like His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ (Ibrahim 14:42).

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Have you not considered﴾ is rhetorical (taqriri), and it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a strengthening for him and a promise of victory, and as an allusion to the obstinate ones, warning them of the like of it. What was done to these three nations is an admonition and a warning to the people who did the same as them, in denying the messengers of Allah. The purpose of it is to bring near the occurrence of that and the expectation of its arrival, because mention of similar cases and calling examples to mind brings close to the minds a matter that seems unlikely to occur; for the long passage of time since the occurrence of its like causes people to forget it, and when it is forgotten, people deem its occurrence improbable. So reminder removes that improbability.

These lessons are particulars of the content of the answer to the oath. If the answer is omitted, then their mention is its indication; and if the answer is His saying ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾, then placing them before the answer serves to increase the suspense toward receiving it, and to announce the kind of the answer before mentioning it, so that after it is mentioned its firm establishment in the minds is increased.

[p. 318]

The seeing in ﴿Have you not considered﴾ may be a seeing of knowledge (ru'ya 'ilmiyya), likening certain knowledge to seeing in clarity and manifestness, because the reports of these nations are widespread and they are proverbially cited, so they are as if witnessed. In that case, kayfa ("how") is an interrogative suspending the verb of seeing from acting upon two objects.

It may also be that the seeing is ocular (basariyya), and the meaning is: "Have you not seen the traces of what your Lord did to ʿĀd?" In that case, kayfa is a noun stripped of interrogative force, in a position of accusative as the object of the ocular seeing.

The divine name (Allah) is replaced by the definition through the addition of "Lord" (Rabb) to the pronoun of the addressee in His saying ﴿your Lord did﴾, because the description "Lord" carries an indication of guardianship and support, and because its addition to the pronoun of the addressee indicates his honour and exaltation.

The admonition begins with the mention of ʿĀd and Thamud because of their fame among the addressees. After them is mentioned the people of Pharaoh, because the message of Musa (peace be upon him) to Pharaoh was famous among the People of the Book in the land of the Arabs, and they used to narrate about it to the Arabs.

By ʿĀd is definitely meant the nation. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those were ʿĀd; they denied the signs of their Lord﴾ (Hud 11:59). The reason it is not diptote (ghayr munsarif) is that it is a triliteral noun with a quiescent middle, like Hind and Nuh. Iram, with a kasra on the hamza and a fatha on the rā', is the name of Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the grandfather of ʿĀd, because ʿĀd is the son of ʿAwS ibn Iram. It is diptote because of foreignness ('ujma), since the extinct Arabs (al-ʿarab al-bA'ida) are considered outside the names of the Arabic language in use. So it is an apposition (ʿaTf bayan) to ʿĀd, to indicate that what is meant by ʿĀd is the tribe whose nearer grandfather is ʿĀd ibn ʿAwS ibn Iram, and he is the ʿĀd described as "the first" in His saying: ﴿And that He destroyed ʿĀd of old﴾ (al-Najm 53:50), lest it be supposed that those spoken of are another tribe also called ʿĀd. They used to dwell in Makkah together with the ʿAmaliq. It is said that they were a remnant of the first ʿĀd, and Iram is a name for the first tribe of ʿĀd.

ʿĀd is described as "of the pillars" (dhat al-ʿimad), and dhat is a feminine descriptive term, because what is meant by ʿĀd is the tribe.

[p. 319]

Al-ʿimad: a thick, tall piece of wood on which a dwelling is erected, planted in the ground, upon which the cloth of a tent or dome is raised; it is called a diʿama (prop). Here it is used metaphorically for strength, likening the strong tribe to the house of pillars.

The use of ʿimad for strength occurs in the verse of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

"And we, when the pillar of the tribe fell upon the baggage, we defend whoever is near us."

It may also be that what is meant by al-ʿimad is the landmarks they built on their roads so that travellers might be guided by them, referred to in His saying: ﴿Do you build on every elevation a landmark, in vain?﴾ (al-Shuʿara 26:128).

ʿĀd is described as "of the pillars" for their strength and might, meaning: Allah has destroyed a people who were mightier than those who denied you. Allah says: ﴿And how many a city was stronger in might than your city which has evicted you—We destroyed them, and they had no helper﴾ (Muhammad 47:13), and He says: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in strength﴾ (Ghafir 40:21).

The relative pronoun alladhi/allati ("which"): it refers to ʿĀd by interpreting it as the tribe, just as ʿĀd was described as "of the pillars." The Arabs say: "Taghlib, the daughter of Wa'il," interpreting Taghlib as the tribe.

Al-bilad: plural of balad and baldah, and it is a wide expanse of land defined by boundaries or inhabitants.

The definite article in al-bilad is for the genus (lil-jins), and the meaning is: "the like of which was not created among the nations in the earth." By creation is meant the creation of their bodies. It is reported that they were tall, sturdy and strong, and that they were people of intellect and management. The Arabs used to coin the proverb about the "forbearance (ahlam) of ʿĀd." Then their natures were corrupted by luxury, and they became insolent toward the blessing.

The apparent meaning is that the article here is for customary generality (istighraq ʿurfi), i.e., in the lands and tribes of the Arabs.

The storytellers (al-qassasun) have fabricated a false tale around His saying ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾. They claimed that "Iram of the pillars" is a compound, made the name of a city in Yemen, or in Syria, or in Egypt, and described its palaces and gardens with unusual attributes. They also fabricated that a Bedouin called ʿAbd Allah ibn Qilaba, in the time of the caliph Muʿawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, wandered in search of his camels and came upon this city; that when he returned he informed the people, and they went to the place where he claimed to have found the city, but found nothing. These are lies mixed with ignorance, for how can its name be "Iram" and be followed by "of the pillars" with the fatha on (Iram) and the kasra on (dhat)? If the name were a compound of the mazji type, the two parts would be indeclinable on the fatha; and if the name were singular and (dhat) an adjective of it, there would be no reason for a kasra on (dhat). Moreover, the position of this name directly after His saying "ʿĀd" contradicts all of that.

Thamud is not declined because what is meant by it is the well-known nation. It is described by the relative pronoun in the plural masculine, in His saying ﴿alladhina jabu﴾ ("who carved"), rather than saying "allati jabat" ("which carved") with the interpretation of a people. Once it was described, the form of the feminine was set aside as a variation in style (tafannun fi al-uslub).

The meaning of jabu is "cut," i.e., they hewed the rock and made houses in it, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you carve out houses from the mountains﴾ (al-Shuʿara 26:149). It has been said that Thamud were the first of the nations of mankind to hew rock and marble. Al-sakhr: great stones.

Al-wad: a name for land lying between two mountains and low-lying; from it the course of abundant water is called a wad. It has two forms: that its last letter is a dal, or that its last letter is a quiescent yā' after the dal.

The majority read it without a yā'. Ibn Kathir and Yaʿqub read it with a yā' at its end both in continuation and in pause. Warsh, on the authority of Nafiʿ, read it with a yā' in continuation and without it in pause. This reading is based on consideration of the verse-endings (fawasil). This is also what preceded in His saying: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ (al-Fajr 89:4). The Mushaf (Qur'an codex) writes it without a yā'. The readings rely on transmission by hearing, not on the orthography of the Mushaf, for the purpose of writing the Mushafs is that the memorisers may be reminded by them of what they might forget.

Al-Wad, as a proper name by dominance, applies to the dwellings of Thamud. It is called Wadi al-Qura, by its attribution to the villages (qura) which Thamud built in it. It is also called al-Hijr, with a kasra on the ḥāʾ and quiescence on the jīm, and it is called Hijr Thamud. It is a valley between Khaybar and Tayma', on the route of one walking from Madinah to Syria. The Jews dwelt in it after Thamud when they settled in the lands of the Arabs, and there settled from the Arab tribes Quda'a, Juhayna, ʿUdhra and Baliyy.

The Prophet (ﷺ) had campaigned against it and conquered it in the seventh year (of Hijra), so those in it from among the Arabs embraced Islam, and the Jews were reconciled upon paying the jizya.

The bā' in His saying (bi'l-wadi) is for location (zarfiyya).

By (Pharaoh) is meant him and his people.

The description (dhi al-awtad, "master of the stakes") is because his kingdom contained the pyramids which his ancestors built, since the shape of a pyramid on the earth resembles a driven stake. It is also possible that (al-awtad) is used metaphorically for firm establishment and stability, meaning: "one of power," in the manner of His saying (dhat al-ʿimad). This was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Before them the people of Noah, and ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, master of the stakes, denied﴾ (Sad 38:12), in Surah Sad.

Al-tughyan: extreme disobedience and injustice. The meaning of their transgression in the lands is that each of these nations transgressed in its own land. Since their land was among the lands, that is, the territories of those peoples, their transgression in their land amounted to transgression in the lands, because the corruption of part leads to the corruption of the whole through establishing evil practices. For this reason, what follows from it is subordinated: ﴿and so they increased corruption therein﴾, because transgression emboldens its doer to violate people's rights. Thus, on one side, he becomes a model of evil for his like and his councillors, so each one of them transgresses against those beneath him, and that is great corruption, since the sacred laws and sound human legislation are thereby disrupted. On another side, it stirs up resentment and rancour in the transgressed-against among the subjects, so they harbour evil toward the transgressors, and their souls hold hatred of the rulers and wait for misfortunes to befall them. Thus they become enemies to them with unsincere hearts, and the men of the state become apprehensive of them out of fear and suspect them of evil in every situation and beware of them. Thus the strength of the nation is dispersed among its individuals instead of being united against its enemies, so the nation has enemies outside and enemies within. That leads to great corruption. Al-fasad: the bad state of a thing and the infliction of harm upon it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:205). Its opposite is reform (al-salah). Here it is used metaphorically for the descent of punishment all at once and its encompassing them, as water is poured upon one who bathes or rain is poured upon the earth. Similar to the pouring is the saying of the Arabs: "He raided them (shanna ʿalayhim al-ghara)."

Thamud—the Cry seized them. As for Pharaoh, they reckoned the sea to be receded, yet nothing alarmed them until it had encompassed them.

That is, God is watchful over every tyrant who causes corruption.

This cannot serve as the answer to the oath. Rather, it is either (1) an indication of the answer (dalil al-jawab), since it shows that what is sworn to is of the same kind as what was done to these three nations, namely the total annihilation (al-isti'sal) indicated by His saying: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. The estimated answer is then: "Your Lord will surely pour upon those who deny you a scourge of punishment, just as He poured it upon ʿĀd, Thamud and Pharaoh."

Or (2) it is a preface and introduction to the answer, if you take the answer to be His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾, and what lies between it and the preceding verses is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) placed as an introduction to the answer of the oath.

The meaning is: your Lord is in observation of the deniers; nothing of their affairs is hidden from Him. This is a strengthening of the Prophet (ﷺ), like His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ (Ibrahim 14:42).

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Have you not considered﴾ is rhetorical (taqriri), and it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a strengthening for him and a promise of victory, and as an allusion to the obstinate ones, warning them of the like of it. What was done to these three nations is an admonition and a warning to the people who did the same as them, in denying the messengers of Allah. The purpose of it is to bring near the occurrence of that and the expectation of its arrival, because mention of similar cases and calling examples to mind brings close to the minds a matter that seems unlikely to occur; for the long passage of time since the occurrence of its like causes people to forget it, and when it is forgotten, people deem its occurrence improbable. So reminder removes that improbability.

If the answer is omitted, then their mention is its indication; and if the answer is His saying ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾, then placing them before the answer serves to increase the suspense toward receiving it, and to announce the kind of the answer before mentioning it, so that after it is mentioned its firm establishment in the minds is increased.

The seeing in ﴿Have you not considered﴾ may be a seeing of knowledge (ru'ya 'ilmiyya), likening certain knowledge to seeing in clarity and manifestness, because the reports of these nations are widespread and they are proverbially cited, so they are as if witnessed. In that case, kayfa ("how") is an interrogative suspending the verb of seeing from acting upon two objects.

It may also be that the seeing is ocular (basariyya), and the meaning is: "Have you not seen the traces of what your Lord did to ʿĀd?" In that case, kayfa is a noun stripped of interrogative force, in a position of accusative as the object of the ocular seeing.

The divine name (Allah) is replaced by the definition through the addition of "Lord" (Rabb) to the pronoun of the addressee in His saying ﴿your Lord did﴾, because the description "Lord" carries an indication of guardianship and support, and because its addition to the pronoun of the addressee indicates his honour and exaltation.

The admonition begins with the mention of ʿĀd and Thamud because of their fame among the addressees. After them is mentioned the people of Pharaoh, because the message of Musa (peace be upon him) to Pharaoh was famous among the People of the Book in the land of the Arabs, and they used to narrate about it to the Arabs.

By ʿĀd is definitely meant the nation. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those were ʿĀd; they denied the signs of their Lord﴾ (Hud 11:59). The reason it is not diptote (ghayr munsarif) is that it is a triliteral noun with a quiescent middle, like Hind and Nuh. Iram, with a kasra on the hamza and a fatha on the rā', is the name of Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the grandfather of ʿĀd, because ʿĀd is the son of ʿAwS ibn Iram. It is diptote because of foreignness ('ujma), since the extinct Arabs (al-ʿarab al-bA'ida) are considered outside the names of the Arabic language in use. So it is an apposition (ʿaTf bayan) to ʿĀd, to indicate that what is meant by ʿĀd is the tribe whose nearer grandfather is ʿĀd ibn ʿAwS ibn Iram, and he is the ʿĀd described as "the first" in His saying: ﴿And that He destroyed ʿĀd of old﴾ (al-Najm 53:50), lest it be supposed that those spoken of are another tribe also called ʿĀd. They used to dwell in Makkah together with the ʿAmaliq. It is said that they were a remnant of the first ʿĀd, and Iram is a name for the first tribe of ʿĀd.

ʿĀd is described as "of the pillars" (dhat al-ʿimad), and dhat is a feminine descriptive term, because what is meant by ʿĀd is the tribe.

[p. 319]

Al-ʿimad: a thick, tall piece of wood on which a dwelling is erected, planted in the ground, upon which the cloth of a tent or dome is raised; it is called a diʿama (prop). Here it is used metaphorically for strength, likening the strong tribe to the house of pillars.

The use of ʿimad for strength occurs in the verse of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

"And we, when the pillar of the tribe fell upon the baggage, we defend whoever is near us."

It may also be that what is meant by al-ʿimad is the landmarks they built on their roads so that travellers might be guided by them, referred to in His saying: ﴿Do you build on every elevation a landmark, in vain?﴾ (al-Shuʿara 26:128).

ʿĀd is described as "of the pillars" for their strength and might, meaning: Allah has destroyed a people who were mightier than those who denied you. Allah says: ﴿And how many a city was stronger in might than your city which has evicted you—We destroyed them, and they had no helper﴾ (Muhammad 47:13), and He says: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in strength﴾ (Ghafir 40:21).

Al-bilad: plural of balad and baldah, and it is a wide expanse of land defined by boundaries or inhabitants.

The definite article in al-bilad is for the genus (lil-jins), and the meaning is: "the like of which was not created among the nations in the earth." By creation is meant the creation of their bodies. It is reported that they were tall, sturdy and strong, and that they were people of intellect and management. The Arabs used to coin the proverb about the "forbearance (ahlam) of ʿĀd." Then their natures were corrupted by luxury, and they became insolent toward the blessing.

The apparent meaning is that the article here is for customary generality (istighraq ʿurfi), i.e., in the lands and tribes of the Arabs.

The storytellers (al-qassasun) have fabricated a false tale around His saying ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾. They claimed that "Iram of the pillars" is a compound, made the name of a city in Yemen, or in Syria, or in Egypt, and described its palaces and gardens with unusual attributes. They also fabricated that a Bedouin called ʿAbd Allah ibn Qilaba, in the time of the caliph Muʿawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, wandered in search of his camels and came upon this city; that when he returned he informed the people, and they went to the place where he claimed to have found the city, but found nothing. These are lies mixed with ignorance, for how can its name be "Iram" and be followed by "of the pillars" with the fatha on (Iram) and the kasra on (dhat)? If the name were a compound of the mazji type, the two parts would be indeclinable on the fatha; and if the name were singular and (dhat) an adjective of it, there would be no reason for a kasra on (dhat). Moreover, the position of this name directly after His saying "ʿĀd" contradicts all of that.

It is described by the relative pronoun in the plural masculine, in His saying ﴿alladhina jabu﴾ ("who carved"), rather than saying "allati jabat" ("which carved") with the interpretation of a people. Once it was described, the form of the feminine was set aside as a variation in style (tafannun fi al-uslub).

The meaning of jabu is "cut," i.e., they hewed the rock and made houses in it, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you carve out houses from the mountains﴾ (al-Shuʿara 26:149). It has been said that Thamud were the first of the nations of mankind to hew rock and marble. Al-sakhr: great stones.

Warsh, on the authority of Nafiʿ, read it with a yā' in continuation and without it in pause. This reading is based on consideration of the verse-endings (fawasil). This is also what preceded in His saying: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ (al-Fajr 89:4). The Mushaf (Qur'an codex) writes it without a yā'. The readings rely on transmission by hearing, not on the orthography of the Mushaf, for the purpose of writing the Mushafs is that the memorisers may be reminded by them of what they might forget.

It is a valley between Khaybar and Tayma', on the route of one walking from Madinah to Syria. The Jews dwelt in it after Thamud when they settled in the lands of the Arabs, and there settled from the Arab tribes Quda'a, Juhayna, ʿUdhra and Baliyy.

The Prophet (ﷺ) had campaigned against it and conquered it in the seventh year (of Hijra), so those in it from among the Arabs embraced Islam, and the Jews were reconciled upon paying the jizya.

Thus, on one side, he becomes a model of evil for his like and his councillors, so each one of them transgresses against those beneath him, and that is great corruption, since the sacred laws and sound human legislation are thereby disrupted. The clause "Indeed your Lord is ever watchful" (inna Rabbaka la-bil-mirsad) serves as a concluding and explanatory statement (tadhyil wa ta'lil) for their being struck with a whip of punishment, if the answer of the oath is taken to be omitted. It may also be the answer of the oath, as was mentioned just above.

On the view that the clause is a concluding statement, it is a causal explanation of the clause "So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment," affirming the Prophet (ﷺ) that God supports His messengers, and openly declaring to the obstinate what was hinted to them of the expectation that He would deal with them in the same manner He dealt with the earlier deniers. That is, God is watchful over every tyrant who causes corruption.

On the view that it is the answer of the oath, it is a metonymy (kinayah) for the imposition of punishment upon the polytheists, since watchfulness (al-rasd) is intended only to repel the aggressor, whether an enemy or otherwise. The sworn matter and what precedes it are then a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad), a stylistic variation in the composition of the speech: placed before the object of the oath is what serves as evidence for it and as a parallel with the punishment of their like among the nations that preceded them, from His saying: "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad..." and so on. This is a mode of rhetorical discourse (khitabah), in which the exposition and parallel are placed in the position of a premise, and the intended purpose is placed in the position of the conclusion and the cause, when the speech is suitable for both considerations, together with the intention of giving attention to the premise and hastening to it.

The shift from the first-person pronoun or the divine name to "your Lord" (Rabbuka) in His saying "So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment" and His saying "Indeed your Lord is ever watchful" indicates that the one who does this is his Lord, whose nature is to give victory to him. Thus he is assured that He will punish those who denied him, giving victory to him as a master gives victory to his client.

Al-mirsad: the place where the watchers (al-rasad) are posted, i.e., the group who observe something. The form mif'al comes for a place, for a time, and as it comes for an instrument; here the sense of instrument is not admissible, so it is here either for time or for place, since al-rasd means watching.

The definiteness of "al-mirsad" is the definiteness of the genus, and it conveys the generality of its object: that He is watchful over every doer. It is thus a figurative depiction of the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of the deeds and movements of His servants, in the manner of sentries observing the movements of an enemy and raiders. This image is a metonymy for requiting each doer for what he has done and does, since watching is intended only for requital for aggression. In what it conveys of causation there is a hint that God did not wrong them in what befell them.

The bā' in His saying "bil-mirsad" is for the sense of place (ẓarfiyyah).

This cannot serve as the answer to the oath. Rather, it is either (1) an indication of the answer (dalil al-jawab), since it shows that what is sworn to is of the same kind as what was done to these three nations, namely the total annihilation (al-isti'sal) indicated by His saying: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. The estimated answer is then: "Your Lord will surely pour upon those who deny you a scourge of punishment, just as He poured it upon ʿĀd, Thamud and Pharaoh."

Or (2) it is a preface and introduction to the answer, if you take the answer to be His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾, and what lies between it and the preceding verses is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) placed as an introduction to the answer of the oath.

The meaning is: your Lord is in observation of the deniers; nothing of their affairs is hidden from Him. This is a strengthening of the Prophet (ﷺ), like His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ (Ibrahim 14:42).

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Have you not considered﴾ is rhetorical (taqriri), and it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a strengthening for him and a promise of victory, and as an allusion to the obstinate ones, warning them of the like of it. What was done to these three nations is an admonition and a warning to the people who did the same as them, in denying the messengers of Allah. The purpose of it is to bring near the occurrence of that and the expectation of its arrival, because mention of similar cases and calling examples to mind brings close to the minds a matter that seems unlikely to occur; for the long passage of time since the occurrence of its like causes people to forget it, and when it is forgotten, people deem its occurrence improbable. So reminder removes that improbability.

These lessons are particulars of the content of the answer to the oath. If the answer is omitted, then their mention is its indication; and if the answer is His saying ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾, then placing them before the answer serves to increase the suspense toward receiving it, and to announce the kind of the answer before mentioning it, so that after it is mentioned its firm establishment in the minds is increased.

The annexation of "sawta" to "adhab" is an annexation of the attribute to the thing described: the sense is "He poured upon them a punishment that was a whip," i.e., like a whip in the swiftness of its striking. It is therefore an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh).

The clause "Indeed your Lord is ever watchful" (inna Rabbaka la-bil-mirsad) serves as a concluding and explanatory statement (tadhyil wa ta'lil) for their being struck with a whip of punishment, if the answer of the oath is taken to be omitted. It may also be the answer of the oath, as was mentioned just above.

On the view that the clause is a concluding statement, it is a causal explanation of the clause "So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment," affirming the Prophet (ﷺ) that God supports His messengers, and openly declaring to the obstinate what was hinted to them of the expectation that He would deal with them in the same manner He dealt with the earlier deniers. That is, God is watchful over every tyrant who causes corruption.

On the view that it is the answer of the oath, it is a metonymy (kinayah) for the imposition of punishment upon the polytheists, since watchfulness (al-rasd) is intended only to repel the aggressor, whether an enemy or otherwise. The sworn matter and what precedes it are then a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad), a stylistic variation in the composition of the speech: placed before the object of the oath is what serves as evidence for it and as a parallel with the punishment of their like among the nations that preceded them, from His saying: "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad..." and so on. This is a mode of rhetorical discourse (khitabah), in which the exposition and parallel are placed in the position of a premise, and the intended purpose is placed in the position of the conclusion and the cause, when the speech is suitable for both considerations, together with the intention of giving attention to the premise and hastening to it.

The shift from the first-person pronoun or the divine name to "your Lord" (Rabbuka) in His saying "So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment" and His saying "Indeed your Lord is ever watchful" indicates that the one who does this is his Lord, whose nature is to give victory to him. Thus he is assured that He will punish those who denied him, giving victory to him as a master gives victory to his client.

Al-mirsad: the place where the watchers (al-rasad) are posted, i.e., the group who observe something. The form mif'al comes for a place, for a time, and as it comes for an instrument; here the sense of instrument is not admissible, so it is here either for time or for place, since al-rasd means watching.

The definiteness of "al-mirsad" is the definiteness of the genus, and it conveys the generality of its object: that He is watchful over every doer. It is thus a figurative depiction of the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of the deeds and movements of His servants, in the manner of sentries observing the movements of an enemy and raiders. This image is a metonymy for requiting each doer for what he has done and does, since watching is intended only for requital for aggression. In what it conveys of causation there is a hint that God did not wrong them in what befell them.

The bā' in His saying "bil-mirsad" is for the sense of place (ẓarfiyyah).

﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd,﴾ ﴿Iram of the pillars,﴾ ﴿the like of which was not created in the lands,﴾ ﴿and Thamud, who carved out the rocks in the valley,﴾ ﴿and Pharaoh, master of the stakes,﴾ ﴿who transgressed in the lands﴾ ﴿and increased corruption therein?﴾ ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation.﴾

This cannot serve as the answer to the oath. Rather, it is either (1) an indication of the answer (dalil al-jawab), since it shows that what is sworn to is of the same kind as what was done to these three nations, namely the total annihilation (al-isti'sal) indicated by His saying: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. The estimated answer is then: "Your Lord will surely pour upon those who deny you a scourge of punishment, just as He poured it upon ʿĀd, Thamud and Pharaoh."

Or (2) it is a preface and introduction to the answer, if you take the answer to be His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾, and what lies between it and the preceding verses is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) placed as an introduction to the answer of the oath.

The meaning is: your Lord is in observation of the deniers; nothing of their affairs is hidden from Him. This is a strengthening of the Prophet (ﷺ), like His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ (Ibrahim 14:42).

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Have you not considered﴾ is rhetorical (taqriri), and it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a strengthening for him and a promise of victory, and as an allusion to the obstinate ones, warning them of the like of it. What was done to these three nations is an admonition and a warning to the people who did the same as them, in denying the messengers of Allah. The purpose of it is to bring near the occurrence of that and the expectation of its arrival, because mention of similar cases and calling examples to mind brings close to the minds a matter that seems unlikely to occur; for the long passage of time since the occurrence of its like causes people to forget it, and when it is forgotten, people deem its occurrence improbable. So reminder removes that improbability.

The seeing in ﴿Have you not considered﴾ may be a seeing of knowledge (ru'ya 'ilmiyya), likening certain knowledge to seeing in clarity and manifestness, because the reports of these nations are widespread and they are proverbially cited, so they are as if witnessed. In that case, kayfa ("how") is an interrogative suspending the verb of seeing from acting upon two objects.

It may also be that the seeing is ocular (basariyya), and the meaning is: "Have you not seen the traces of what your Lord did to ʿĀd?" In that case, kayfa is a noun stripped of interrogative force, in a position of accusative as the object of the ocular seeing.

The divine name (Allah) is replaced by the definition through the addition of "Lord" (Rabb) to the pronoun of the addressee in His saying ﴿your Lord did﴾, because the description "Lord" carries an indication of guardianship and support, and because its addition to the pronoun of the addressee indicates his honour and exaltation.

The admonition begins with the mention of ʿĀd and Thamud because of their fame among the addressees. After them is mentioned the people of Pharaoh, because the message of Musa (peace be upon him) to Pharaoh was famous among the People of the Book in the land of the Arabs, and they used to narrate about it to the Arabs.

By ʿĀd is definitely meant the nation. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those were ʿĀd; they denied the signs of their Lord﴾ (Hud 11:59). The reason it is not diptote (ghayr munsarif) is that it is a triliteral noun with a quiescent middle, like Hind and Nuh. Iram, with a kasra on the hamza and a fatha on the rā', is the name of Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the grandfather of ʿĀd, because ʿĀd is the son of ʿAwS ibn Iram. They used to dwell in Makkah together with the ʿAmaliq. It is said that they were a remnant of the first ʿĀd, and Iram is a name for the first tribe of ʿĀd.

ʿĀd is described as "of the pillars" (dhat al-ʿimad), and dhat is a feminine descriptive term, because what is meant by ʿĀd is the tribe.

[p. 319]

Al-ʿimad: a thick, tall piece of wood on which a dwelling is erected, planted in the ground, upon which the cloth of a tent or dome is raised; it is called a diʿama (prop). Here it is used metaphorically for strength, likening the strong tribe to the house of pillars.

The use of ʿimad for strength occurs in the verse of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

"And we, when the pillar of the tribe fell upon the baggage, we defend whoever is near us."

It may also be that what is meant by al-ʿimad is the landmarks they built on their roads so that travellers might be guided by them, referred to in His saying: ﴿Do you build on every elevation a landmark, in vain?﴾ (al-Shuʿara 26:128).

ʿĀd is described as "of the pillars" for their strength and might, meaning: Allah has destroyed a people who were mightier than those who denied you. Allah says: ﴿And how many a city was stronger in might than your city which has evicted you—We destroyed them, and they had no helper﴾ (Muhammad 47:13), and He says: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? They were greater than them in strength﴾ (Ghafir 40:21).

Al-bilad: plural of balad and baldah, and it is a wide expanse of land defined by boundaries or inhabitants.

The definite article in al-bilad is for the genus (lil-jins), and the meaning is: "the like of which was not created among the nations in the earth." By creation is meant the creation of their bodies. It is reported that they were tall, sturdy and strong, and that they were people of intellect and management. The Arabs used to coin the proverb about the "forbearance (ahlam) of ʿĀd." Then their natures were corrupted by luxury, and they became insolent toward the blessing.

The apparent meaning is that the article here is for customary generality (istighraq ʿurfi), i.e., in the lands and tribes of the Arabs.

They claimed that "Iram of the pillars" is a compound, made the name of a city in Yemen, or in Syria, or in Egypt, and described its palaces and gardens with unusual attributes. These are lies mixed with ignorance, for how can its name be "Iram" and be followed by "of the pillars" with the fatha on (Iram) and the kasra on (dhat)? If the name were a compound of the mazji type, the two parts would be indeclinable on the fatha; and if the name were singular and (dhat) an adjective of it, there would be no reason for a kasra on (dhat). It is described by the relative pronoun in the plural masculine, in His saying ﴿alladhina jabu﴾ ("who carved"), rather than saying "allati jabat" ("which carved") with the interpretation of a people. Once it was described, the form of the feminine was set aside as a variation in style (tafannun fi al-uslub).

The meaning of jabu is "cut," i.e., they hewed the rock and made houses in it, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And you carve out houses from the mountains﴾ (al-Shuʿara 26:149). It has been said that Thamud were the first of the nations of mankind to hew rock and marble. Al-sakhr: great stones.

Warsh, on the authority of Nafiʿ, read it with a yā' in continuation and without it in pause. This reading is based on consideration of the verse-endings (fawasil). This is also what preceded in His saying: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾ (al-Fajr 89:4). The Mushaf (Qur'an codex) writes it without a yā'. The readings rely on transmission by hearing, not on the orthography of the Mushaf, for the purpose of writing the Mushafs is that the memorisers may be reminded by them of what they might forget.

Al-Wad, as a proper name by dominance, applies to the dwellings of Thamud. It is called Wadi al-Qura, by its attribution to the villages (qura) which Thamud built in it. It is also called al-Hijr, with a kasra on the ḥāʾ and quiescence on the jīm, and it is called Hijr Thamud. It is a valley between Khaybar and Tayma', on the route of one walking from Madinah to Syria. The Jews dwelt in it after Thamud when they settled in the lands of the Arabs, and there settled from the Arab tribes Quda'a, Juhayna, ʿUdhra and Baliyy.

[p. 320]

[p. 321]

The Prophet (ﷺ) had campaigned against it and conquered it in the seventh year (of Hijra), so those in it from among the Arabs embraced Islam, and the Jews were reconciled upon paying the jizya.

The bā' in His saying (bi'l-wadi) is for location (zarfiyya).

By (Pharaoh) is meant him and his people.

The description (dhi al-awtad, "master of the stakes") is because his kingdom contained the pyramids which his ancestors built, since the shape of a pyramid on the earth resembles a driven stake. It is also possible that (al-awtad) is used metaphorically for firm establishment and stability, meaning: "one of power," in the manner of His saying (dhat al-ʿimad). This was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Before them the people of Noah, and ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, master of the stakes, denied﴾ (Sad 38:12), in Surah Sad.

His saying ﴿who transgressed in the lands﴾ may include all those mentioned: ʿĀd, Thamud and Pharaoh. It may also be a qualifier of Pharaoh, since what is meant is him and his people.

Al-tughyan: extreme disobedience and injustice. The meaning of their transgression in the lands is that each of these nations transgressed in its own land. Since their land was among the lands, that is, the territories of those peoples, their transgression in their land amounted to transgression in the lands, because the corruption of part leads to the corruption of the whole through establishing evil practices. For this reason, what follows from it is subordinated: ﴿and so they increased corruption therein﴾, because transgression emboldens its doer to violate people's rights. Thus, on one side, he becomes a model of evil for his like and his councillors, so each one of them transgresses against those beneath him, and that is great corruption, since the sacred laws and sound human legislation are thereby disrupted. On another side, it stirs up resentment and rancour in the transgressed-against among the subjects, so they harbour evil toward the transgressors, and their souls hold hatred of the rulers and wait for misfortunes to befall them. Thus they become enemies to them with unsincere hearts, and the men of the state become apprehensive of them out of fear and suspect them of evil in every situation and beware of them. Thus the strength of the nation is dispersed among its individuals instead of being united against its enemies, so the nation has enemies outside and enemies within. That leads to great corruption. Therefore transgression was indeed a cause of the multiplication of corruption.

It is also possible that the definite article in (al-bilad) is the definite article of prior reference (ʿahd), i.e., "in their lands," and the plural is according to the consideration of distribution, i.e., each nation transgressed in its own land.

[p. 322]

Al-fasad: the bad state of a thing and the infliction of harm upon it. What they had multiplied of corruption was a cause of Allah's anger upon them, and Allah does not love corruption; so He poured upon them the punishment.

Here it is used metaphorically for the descent of punishment all at once and its encompassing them, as water is poured upon one who bathes or rain is poured upon the earth. Similar to the pouring is the saying of the Arabs: "He raided them (shanna ʿalayhim al-ghara)."

The punishment which befell these people was a sudden and decisive punishment.

As for ʿĀd, they saw a cloud forming on the horizon and thought it a cloud of rain, but they had not stayed long before the wind carried them away, every one of them.

Thamud—the Cry seized them. As for Pharaoh, they reckoned the sea to be receded, yet nothing alarmed them until it had encompassed them.

[p. 320]

[p. 321]

The Prophet (ﷺ) had campaigned against it and conquered it in the seventh year (of Hijra), so those in it from among the Arabs embraced Islam, and the Jews were reconciled upon paying the jizya.

The bā' in His saying (bi'l-wadi) is for location (zarfiyya).

By (Pharaoh) is meant him and his people.

The description (dhi al-awtad, "master of the stakes") is because his kingdom contained the pyramids which his ancestors built, since the shape of a pyramid on the earth resembles a driven stake. It is also possible that (al-awtad) is used metaphorically for firm establishment and stability, meaning: "one of power," in the manner of His saying (dhat al-ʿimad). This was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Before them the people of Noah, and ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, master of the stakes, denied﴾ (Sad 38:12), in Surah Sad.

His saying ﴿who transgressed in the lands﴾ may include all those mentioned: ʿĀd, Thamud and Pharaoh. It may also be a qualifier of Pharaoh, since what is meant is him and his people.

Al-tughyan: extreme disobedience and injustice. The meaning of their transgression in the lands is that each of these nations transgressed in its own land. Since their land was among the lands, that is, the territories of those peoples, their transgression in their land amounted to transgression in the lands, because the corruption of part leads to the corruption of the whole through establishing evil practices. For this reason, what follows from it is subordinated: ﴿and so they increased corruption therein﴾, because transgression emboldens its doer to violate people's rights. Thus, on one side, he becomes a model of evil for his like and his councillors, so each one of them transgresses against those beneath him, and that is great corruption, since the sacred laws and sound human legislation are thereby disrupted. On another side, it stirs up resentment and rancour in the transgressed-against among the subjects, so they harbour evil toward the transgressors, and their souls hold hatred of the rulers and wait for misfortunes to befall them. Thus they become enemies to them with unsincere hearts, and the men of the state become apprehensive of them out of fear and suspect them of evil in every situation and beware of them. Thus the strength of the nation is dispersed among its individuals instead of being united against its enemies, so the nation has enemies outside and enemies within. That leads to great corruption. Therefore transgression was indeed a cause of the multiplication of corruption.

[p. 322]

Al-fasad: the bad state of a thing and the infliction of harm upon it. What they had multiplied of corruption was a cause of Allah's anger upon them, and Allah does not love corruption; so He poured upon them the punishment.

Here it is used metaphorically for the descent of punishment all at once and its encompassing them, as water is poured upon one who bathes or rain is poured upon the earth. The point of resemblance is composed of speed and abundance. Similar is the metaphor of pouring (ifrigh) in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:250). Similar to the pouring is the saying of the Arabs: "He raided them (shanna ʿalayhim al-ghara)."

The punishment which befell these people was a sudden and decisive punishment.

As for ʿĀd, they saw a cloud forming on the horizon and thought it a cloud of rain, but they had not stayed long before the wind carried them away, every one of them.

Thamud—the Cry seized them. As for Pharaoh, they reckoned the sea to be receded, yet nothing alarmed them until it had encompassed them.

That is, God is watchful over every tyrant who causes corruption.

Thus he is assured that He will punish those who denied him, giving victory to him as a master gives victory to his client.

Al-mirsad: the place where the watchers (al-rasad) are posted, i.e., the group who observe something. In what it conveys of causation there is a hint that God did not wrong them in what befell them.

The bā' in His saying "bil-mirsad" is for the sense of place (ẓarfiyyah).

This cannot serve as the answer to the oath. Rather, it is either (1) an indication of the answer (dalil al-jawab), since it shows that what is sworn to is of the same kind as what was done to these three nations, namely the total annihilation (al-isti'sal) indicated by His saying: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. The estimated answer is then: "Your Lord will surely pour upon those who deny you a scourge of punishment, just as He poured it upon ʿĀd, Thamud and Pharaoh."

Or (2) it is a preface and introduction to the answer, if you take the answer to be His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾, and what lies between it and the preceding verses is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) placed as an introduction to the answer of the oath.

The meaning is: your Lord is in observation of the deniers; nothing of their affairs is hidden from Him. This is a strengthening of the Prophet (ﷺ), like His saying: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾ (Ibrahim 14:42).

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Have you not considered﴾ is rhetorical (taqriri), and it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a strengthening for him and a promise of victory, and as an allusion to the obstinate ones, warning them of the like of it. What was done to these three nations is an admonition and a warning to the people who did the same as them, in denying the messengers of Allah. The purpose of it is to bring near the occurrence of that and the expectation of its arrival, because mention of similar cases and calling examples to mind brings close to the minds a matter that seems unlikely to occur; for the long passage of time since the occurrence of its like causes people to forget it, and when it is forgotten, people deem its occurrence improbable. So reminder removes that improbability.

These lessons are particulars of the content of the answer to the oath. If the answer is omitted, then their mention is its indication; and if the answer is His saying ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation﴾, then placing them before the answer serves to increase the suspense toward receiving it, and to announce the kind of the answer before mentioning it, so that after it is mentioned its firm establishment in the minds is increased.

[p. 318]

The seeing in ﴿Have you not considered﴾ may be a seeing of knowledge (ru'ya 'ilmiyya), likening certain knowledge to seeing in clarity and manifestness, because the reports of these nations are widespread and they are proverbially cited, so they are as if witnessed. In that case, kayfa ("how") is an interrogative suspending the verb of seeing from acting upon two objects.

It may also be that the seeing is ocular (basariyya), and the meaning is: "Have you not seen the traces of what your Lord did to ʿĀd?" In that case, kayfa is a noun stripped of interrogative force, in a position of accusative as the object of the ocular seeing.

The divine name (Allah) is replaced by the definition through the addition of "Lord" (Rabb) to the pronoun of the addressee in His saying ﴿your Lord did﴾, because the description "Lord" carries an indication of guardianship and support, and because its addition to the pronoun of the addressee indicates his honour and exaltation.

The admonition begins with the mention of ʿĀd and Thamud because of their fame among the addressees. After them is mentioned the people of Pharaoh, because the message of Musa (peace be upon him) to Pharaoh was famous among the People of the Book in the land of the Arabs, and they used to narrate about it to the Arabs.

By ʿĀd is definitely meant the nation. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those were ʿĀd; they denied the signs of their Lord﴾ (Hud 11:59). The reason it is not diptote (ghayr munsarif) is that it is a triliteral noun with a quiescent middle, like Hind and Nuh. Iram, with a kasra on the hamza and a fatha on the rā', is the name of Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he is the grandfather of ʿĀd, because ʿĀd is the son of ʿAwS ibn Iram. It is diptote because of foreignness ('ujma), since the extinct Arabs (al-ʿarab al-bA'ida) are considered outside the names of the Arabic language in use. So it is an apposition (ʿaTf bayan) to ʿĀd, to indicate that what is meant by ʿĀd is the tribe whose nearer grandfather is ʿĀd ibn ʿAwS ibn Iram, and he is the ʿĀd described as "the first" in His saying: ﴿And that He destroyed ʿĀd of old﴾ (al-Najm 53:50), lest it be supposed that those spoken of are another tribe also called ʿĀd. They used to dwell in Makkah together with the ʿAmaliq. It is said that they were a remnant of the first ʿĀd, and Iram is a name for the first tribe of ʿĀd.

ʿĀd is described as "of the pillars" (dhat al-ʿimad), and dhat is a feminine descriptive term, because what is meant by ʿĀd is the tribe.

Al-ʿimad: a thick, tall piece of wood on which a dwelling is erected, planted in the ground, upon which the cloth of a tent or dome is raised; it is called a diʿama (prop). Here it is used metaphorically for strength, likening the strong tribe to the house of pillars.

The use of ʿimad for strength occurs in the verse of ʿAmr ibn Kulthum:

"And we, when the pillar of the tribe fell upon the baggage, we defend whoever is near us."

It may also be that what is meant by al-ʿimad is the landmarks they built on their roads so that travellers might be guided by them, referred to in His saying: ﴿Do you build on every elevation a landmark, in vain?﴾ (al-Shuʿara 26:128).

The Prophet (ﷺ) had campaigned against it and conquered it in the seventh year (of Hijra), so those in it from among the Arabs embraced Islam, and the Jews were reconciled upon paying the jizya.

Thus, on one side, he becomes a model of evil for his like and his councillors, so each one of them transgresses against those beneath him, and that is great corruption, since the sacred laws and sound human legislation are thereby disrupted. On another side, it stirs up resentment and rancour in the transgressed-against among the subjects, so they harbour evil toward the transgressors, and their souls hold hatred of the rulers and wait for misfortunes to befall them. Thus they become enemies to them with unsincere hearts, and the men of the state become apprehensive of them out of fear and suspect them of evil in every situation and beware of them. As for ʿĀd, they saw a cloud forming on the horizon and thought it a cloud of rain, but they had not stayed long before the wind carried them away, every one of them.

Thamud—the Cry seized them. As for Pharaoh, they reckoned the sea to be receded, yet nothing alarmed them until it had encompassed them.

It may also be the answer of the oath, as was mentioned just above.

That is, God is watchful over every tyrant who causes corruption.

This is a mode of rhetorical discourse (khitabah), in which the exposition and parallel are placed in the position of a premise, and the intended purpose is placed in the position of the conclusion and the cause, when the speech is suitable for both considerations, together with the intention of giving attention to the premise and hastening to it.

The shift from the first-person pronoun or the divine name to "your Lord" (Rabbuka) in His saying "So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment" and His saying "Indeed your Lord is ever watchful" indicates that the one who does this is his Lord, whose nature is to give victory to him. Thus he is assured that He will punish those who denied him, giving victory to him as a master gives victory to his client.

Al-mirsad: the place where the watchers (al-rasad) are posted, i.e., the group who observe something. The form mif'al comes for a place, for a time, and as it comes for an instrument; here the sense of instrument is not admissible, so it is here either for time or for place, since al-rasd means watching.

The definiteness of "al-mirsad" is the definiteness of the genus, and it conveys the generality of its object: that He is watchful over every doer. It is thus a figurative depiction of the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of the deeds and movements of His servants, in the manner of sentries observing the movements of an enemy and raiders. This image is a metonymy for requiting each doer for what he has done and does, since watching is intended only for requital for aggression. In what it conveys of causation there is a hint that God did not wrong them in what befell them.

The bā' in His saying "bil-mirsad" is for the sense of place (ẓarfiyyah).
