His saying ﴿who transgressed in the lands﴾ may include all those mentioned: ʿĀd, Thamud and Pharaoh. It may also be a qualifier of Pharaoh, since what is meant is him and his people.

Al-tughyan: extreme disobedience and injustice. The meaning of their transgression in the lands is that each of these nations transgressed in its own land. Since their land was among the lands, that is, the territories of those peoples, their transgression in their land amounted to transgression in the lands, because the corruption of part leads to the corruption of the whole through establishing evil practices. For this reason, what follows from it is subordinated: ﴿and so they increased corruption therein﴾, because transgression emboldens its doer to violate people's rights. Thus, on one side, he becomes a model of evil for his like and his councillors, so each one of them transgresses against those beneath him, and that is great corruption, since the sacred laws and sound human legislation are thereby disrupted. On another side, it stirs up resentment and rancour in the transgressed-against among the subjects, so they harbour evil toward the transgressors, and their souls hold hatred of the rulers and wait for misfortunes to befall them. Thus they become enemies to them with unsincere hearts, and the men of the state become apprehensive of them out of fear and suspect them of evil in every situation and beware of them. Thus the strength of the nation is dispersed among its individuals instead of being united against its enemies, so the nation has enemies outside and enemies within. That leads to great corruption. Therefore transgression was indeed a cause of the multiplication of corruption.

It is also possible that the definite article in (al-bilad) is the definite article of prior reference (ʿahd), i.e., "in their lands," and the plural is according to the consideration of distribution, i.e., each nation transgressed in its own land.

[p. 322]

Al-fasad: the bad state of a thing and the infliction of harm upon it. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:205). Its opposite is reform (al-salah). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾ (al-Araf 7:56). What they had multiplied of corruption was a cause of Allah's anger upon them, and Allah does not love corruption; so He poured upon them the punishment.

Al-sabb in its real sense is the pouring out of what is in a vessel. Here it is used metaphorically for the descent of punishment all at once and its encompassing them, as water is poured upon one who bathes or rain is poured upon the earth. The point of resemblance is composed of speed and abundance. Similar is the metaphor of pouring (ifrigh) in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:250). Similar to the pouring is the saying of the Arabs: "He raided them (shanna ʿalayhim al-ghara)."

The punishment which befell these people was a sudden and decisive punishment.

As for ʿĀd, they saw a cloud forming on the horizon and thought it a cloud of rain, but they had not stayed long before the wind carried them away, every one of them.

Thamud—the Cry seized them. As for Pharaoh, they reckoned the sea to be receded, yet nothing alarmed them until it had encompassed them.

Al-saw† (the whip) is an instrument of striking made of plaited hides, with which horses are struck for discipline and to urge them to greater speed in running.

It is related from al-Farra' that the expression "a whip of punishment" (sawta 'adhab) is used by the Arabs for any punishment that involves the whip (i.e., that befalls by means of the whip). He meant that this is its literal sense, not that it carries this meaning in this verse.

The annexation of "sawta" to "adhab" is an annexation of the attribute to the thing described: the sense is "He poured upon them a punishment that was a whip," i.e., like a whip in the swiftness of its striking. It is therefore an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh).

The clause "Indeed your Lord is ever watchful" (inna Rabbaka la-bil-mirsad) serves as a concluding and explanatory statement (tadhyil wa ta'lil) for their being struck with a whip of punishment, if the answer of the oath is taken to be omitted. It may also be the answer of the oath, as was mentioned just above.

On the view that the clause is a concluding statement, it is a causal explanation of the clause "So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment," affirming the Prophet (ﷺ) that God supports His messengers, and openly declaring to the obstinate what was hinted to them of the expectation that He would deal with them in the same manner He dealt with the earlier deniers. That is, God is watchful over every tyrant who causes corruption.

On the view that it is the answer of the oath, it is a metonymy (kinayah) for the imposition of punishment upon the polytheists, since watchfulness (al-rasd) is intended only to repel the aggressor, whether an enemy or otherwise. The sworn matter and what precedes it are then a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad), a stylistic variation in the composition of the speech: placed before the object of the oath is what serves as evidence for it and as a parallel with the punishment of their like among the nations that preceded them, from His saying: "Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad..." and so on. This is a mode of rhetorical discourse (khitabah), in which the exposition and parallel are placed in the position of a premise, and the intended purpose is placed in the position of the conclusion and the cause, when the speech is suitable for both considerations, together with the intention of giving attention to the premise and hastening to it.

The shift from the first-person pronoun or the divine name to "your Lord" (Rabbuka) in His saying "So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment" and His saying "Indeed your Lord is ever watchful" indicates that the one who does this is his Lord, whose nature is to give victory to him. Thus he is assured that He will punish those who denied him, giving victory to him as a master gives victory to his client.

Al-mirsad: the place where the watchers (al-rasad) are posted, i.e., the group who observe something. The form mif'al comes for a place, for a time, and as it comes for an instrument; here the sense of instrument is not admissible, so it is here either for time or for place, since al-rasd means watching.

The definiteness of "al-mirsad" is the definiteness of the genus, and it conveys the generality of its object: that He is watchful over every doer. It is thus a figurative depiction of the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge of the deeds and movements of His servants, in the manner of sentries observing the movements of an enemy and raiders. This image is a metonymy for requiting each doer for what he has done and does, since watching is intended only for requital for aggression. In what it conveys of causation there is a hint that God did not wrong them in what befell them.

The bā' in His saying "bil-mirsad" is for the sense of place (ẓarfiyyah).

[Page 324]

**﴿Then as for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and blesses him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me." But when He tests him and restricts his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me." No!﴾** (al-Fajr 89:15–17)

The *fa'* (the particle of consequence) indicates that the speech following it is connected to what precedes it and is necessarily derived from it.

The particle *amma* ("as for") conveys the meaning "whatever may be the case," and this is the basic meaning of the particle and what its usage requires. Its use strengthens the connection of its response to what precedes it and to the *fa'* attached to it. This connection shines out like a flash of lightning, and its brilliance clarifies what was obscure, since the derivation of what follows this *fa'* from what precedes it is hidden. So let us explain it clearly.

The preceding discourse described the enjoyments that the nations mentioned were given by God, who bestowed blessings upon them, while they were heedless of the call of God's messengers, turned away from seeking the pleasure of their Lord, plunged into the evils they had been forbidden, were insolent in their blessings, and were self-admiring in their greatness. Therefore, after mentioning what they were doing and what God requited them with in the form of punishment in this world, the discourse draws a lesson, which is to remind the polytheists that their condition is similar to theirs in luxury, rebellion and insolence, and to warn them of their error. For they had, from their state of luxury and blessing, a semblance upon which they built the delusion that God had made them objects of honour. Thus they reckoned that the Messenger's (ﷺ) warning them of punishment was not true, since it contradicted what they were actually experiencing of blessing. So they imagined that God's treatment of them was a stronger proof of their honour in His sight than what the Messenger (ﷺ) reported, namely that God had commanded them to the opposite of what they were doing. They denied that there could be another world after this one that would contradict it, and they restricted God's giving to what His servants have in this worldly life. This delusion thus led them to deny what they were warned of by way of threat, and the reward in the Hereafter that delights the believers. They confined the recompense of good to wealth and blessing, and confined the recompense of evil to poverty and the restriction of provision.

The Qur'an has repeatedly addressed the refutation of this, as in His saying: ﴿Do they suppose that what We supply them with of wealth and children is [a sign that] We hasten for them good things? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:55–56).

This delusion contains principles upon which the denial of recompense in the Hereafter is built, the denial of a second life, and the assumption that conditions will endure forever.

[Page 325]

So the *fa'* of consequence is linked to the sentence ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ (al-Fajr 89:14), with the generality it contains, which is required by its being a concluding statement (*tadhyil*).

The meaning is: this is the way of your Lord, operating in accordance with His knowledge and wisdom. As for the disbelieving man, he imagines otherwise, since he supposes that the blessing and abundance he receives in this world is an honouring from God to him, and that the narrowness of livelihood he receives is a humiliation with which God has humiliated him.

This delusion entails their thinking that God's acts occur without wisdom. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after some hardship had touched him, he would surely say, "This is my due, and I do not think the Hour will ever come. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him." So We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment.﴾ (Fussilat 41:50).

So God informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of the true reality, and alerted them to avoid confusing the fine and lofty proofs, and to avoid making fancy and whim the judge. He reminded them that worldly conditions are fleeting accidents, varying in length and brevity. In all of this is a refutation of the creed of the people of polytheism and their error, which was prevalent among the people of the *Jahiliyya* (the Age of Ignorance). For this reason Nabigha said about the family of Ghassan, who were not polytheists but adhered to Christianity:

*Their assembly is the protection of God, and their religion is upright, so they hope for nothing but the consequences.*
*And they do not reckon good to be without evil after it, nor do they reckon evil to be an inescapable blow.*

God has followed this with rebuke and refutation through His saying "No!" The basis of the rebuke and refutation is both of the two statements, because they both proceed from a false interpretation and a misguided doubt, as you will know when we reach His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then He honoured him and blessed him﴾.

The verse is restricted to the constriction of provision in contrast to blessing, and not to other causes and afflictions, because the majority of the conditions of the polytheists being spoken of were soundness of temperament and strength of bodies. So they did not perish except by killing or old age among them and their relatives. Nabigha said:

*It covers destructions that will not let you wait for old age.*

[Page 326]

Most of the exegetes did not pause to explain the arrangement (*nazm*) of the verse and its connection to what precedes it, except al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya.

This misguided belief is known from the speech of the people of the *Jahiliyya*. Tarafa said:

*Had my Lord willed, I would have been Qays ibn 'Asim,*
*and had my Lord willed, I would have been 'Amr ibn Murthid.*
*So I became possessed of much wealth, and noble sons surrounded me, lords over those who would be lords.*

They made this deception a measure of the ranks of people. They made the people of perfection those with splendid appearances, and they branded the people of poverty and the weak as deficient. For this reason, when the chiefs of Quraysh and of Banu Tamim and Fazara came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while 'Ammar, Bilal, Khabbab, Salim (the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa), Suhayb, and Sabih (the freedman of Usayd), along with other weak believers, were with him, they said to the Prophet: "Drive them away from you, for perhaps if you drive them away, we would follow you." They also said to Abu Talib: "If your nephew were to drive away these slaves and allies, it would be greater in our eyes and more inclined to make us follow him." It was concerning this that God revealed His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ (al-An'am 6:52), the verse as already mentioned in Surat al-An'am.

So God alerted them to the error of their belief by way of mention of its like among what the nations before them believed, which was the cause that made the punishment pour down upon them. He informed them that the conditions of this world are taken as a basis in considering the recompense for deeds, and that the consistent recompense is the recompense of the Day of Resurrection.

The intended meaning of *al-insan* ("man") is the species, and its definiteness is the definiteness of the species, so it encompasses the individuals of the species. However, this is a customary generality, by which is meant the polytheistic people, since they were the majority among the people being spoken of. This is the predominant usage of the word *insan* in the Qur'an revealed at Mecca, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, man transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ (al-'Alaq 96:6); ﴿Does man suppose that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ (al-Qiyamah 75:3); ﴿We have certainly created man in hardship﴾ and ﴿Does he think that no one has power over him?﴾ (al-Balad 90:4–5), and similar verses. This is supported by His saying: ﴿On that day man will remember, but how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾ (al-Fajr 89:23), and the verse continues.

It has been said that a specific individual was intended: it was said to be 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, or Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira, according to Ibn 'Abbas; and it was said to be Umayya ibn Khalaf, according to Muqatil and al-Kalbi; and it was said to be Ubayy ibn Khalaf, also according to al-Kalbi. But these named individuals are merely examples of misguidance. Ibn 'Atiyya said:

[Page 327]

Since this was predominant among the disbelievers, the reproach in this verse came with the name of the species, since (as is the case) some of the believers may fall into something of this tendency.

Know that among the misguidance of the people of polytheism, and among the temptation of Satan for some ignorant believers, is that there is imagined for them what befalls someone, by attributing it to God's arrangement of the connection of effects to their causes and of caused things to their causes. They therefore place whatever fortunate event befalls one of them into the position of an honour from God toward the one who has encountered the benefits of it, following fancy, self-love, conjecture about the unseen, and presumption against God. And when one of them encounters an event that brings him harm, he imagines it, through his delusions, to be a vengeance from God directed at him, out of pessimism on their part.

Those who claimed that the blessing they received from God was an honouring from God to them are not worthy of God's honour.

And those who imagined that what befell them of scarcity of provision was a humiliation from God to them are not lower in God's sight than those who claimed that God had honoured them with the blessing they are in.

This belief caused the polytheists to be deeply immersed in their polytheism, and diverted their gaze from reflecting on what contradicts it. Satanic whisperings have often become a temptation for some weak believers, short-sighted people, and those ignorant of the true creed, as Ahmad ibn al-Rawandi revealed about the instability of their understanding and the scarcity of their knowledge, in his saying:

*How many a wise person whose paths have baffled him,*
*and a fool, a fool, whom you find provided for!*
*This is what has left minds bewildered,*
*and turned the knowledgeable, expert scholar into a heretic.*

This is what diverted the misguided from seeking the truths from their proofs, and diverted them from reflecting on what brings its possessor the pleasure of God and what brings about His anger. The knowledge of God is vast, and His dispositions are varied, and all of them proceed from wisdom: ﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:255). Harm may come to the servant from several causes, and benefit may come from others. Some of this operates openly in the customary way, and some of it bears the mark of breaking customs. Calamities often come from the directions of benefits, and the one who is granted success is alert to the signs. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair﴾ (al-An'am 6:44). And He said: ﴿We did not send a prophet into any town without seizing its people with adversity and hardship, so that they might humble themselves﴾ (al-A'raf 7:94). ﴿Then We exchanged the bad state for good until they multiplied and said, "Hardship and ease touched our fathers too," so We seized them suddenly while they were unaware﴾ (al-A'raf 7:95). And He said: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested once or twice every year, yet they do not repent nor take heed?﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:126).

[Page 328]

The dispositions of God are similar in nature. Some of them indicate His purpose concerning people, and some of them proceed according to the order of the world that He has decreed. Everything has been decreed and determined by Him, His knowledge preceded it, and He connected its effects to their causes, directly or through an intermediary or intermediaries. The one who has insight takes precaution for himself and his people, does not speak about God what his fancy dictates to him when his proofs do not support it, and entrusts what is unclear to him to the knowledge of God.

The condition of these people reported here is not the condition of the Muslims who are guided by the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) and who have insight into the courses of divine dispositions. We may find among the common folk and those who resemble them among the heedless some remnants of the belief of the people of the *Jahiliyya*, in producing the imaginings that their minds dictate to them. So it is incumbent upon them to take admonition from God's admonition in this verse.

Indeed, God may hasten the recompense of good for some of His righteous servants, as He said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ (al-Nahl 16:97). He may also hasten punishment for whomever of His servants He is angry with. He related the words of Noah to his people: ﴿So I said, "Seek forgiveness of your Lord; indeed, He is ever forgiving. He will send down rain upon you in abundance, and provide you with wealth and children"﴾ (Nuh 71:10–12). And He said: ﴿And if they had remained upright on the way, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ (al-Jinn 72:16). This treatment has signs, the most evident of which is that it proceeds contrary to what is customary, as we see in the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the caliphs over great and dominant nations. These are promises from God which He fulfils, or a threat from Him that befalls those who deserve it.

The particle *amma* generally indicates detail, that is, it points to a contrast between two things, whether of essences or of states. For this reason it is repeated in speech. The detail it conveys is not in the sense of clarifying a preceding ambiguity; rather, it is detail, contrast, and balance. This is one of the kinds of detail for which *amma* is used. The connection of the detail to the preceding speech is conveyed by the *fa'* that enters upon *amma*, and its connection to what precedes it is the connection of a derived matter to its source, not a detailed explanation of a general statement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 89, verses 15–16 (part 2 of 2):

[p. 330]

The detail here concerns the states of the ignorant human being. It is explained by his state in ease and comfort, and his state in hardship and distress. The balance between the two states, expressed by the two time clauses in His words (﴿When his Lord tests him and honours him﴾), and in His words (﴿As for when He tests him and restricts his provision﴾), and so on. This detailing is not of the kind that clarifies what is general (mujmal). Rather, it is a distinguishing and separating between two things, or things that resemble each other or become confused.

The particle (أمّا, ʾammā, "as for") has already been discussed at His words, exalted is He: (﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]), in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-ibtila' (الابتلاء, "testing") means examination, and it occurs through good and through harm, because in both there is a test of the steadfastness of the soul, and of the disposition of forbearance and patience. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35]). By mentioning the testing it becomes clear that God's honouring of him is a honouring that is a test, so it falls into two states: a state that is pleasing (to God) and a state that is not pleasing. Likewise, the restriction of provision is a restriction of testing, which also requires two states. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿That He may test me, whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Naml: 40]), and He said: (﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35]). The more common usage is that testing is by harm, but in this verse it is used in both senses.

The meaning is: when his Lord makes what reaches him of blessing, or of restriction, a manifestation of his state in gratitude and ingratitude, and in patience and impatience, he imagines that God has honoured him by that, or humiliated him by this.

On al-ikram (الإكرام, "honouring"), al-Raghib said: "It is that a dignity (karamah) reaches a person, and it is a benefit in which there is no shame or humiliation; and that he makes what reaches him something noble (karim), i.e., honourable. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]), i.e., He made them noble." End of quotation. He means that honouring is applied to giving a dignity, and it is also applied to making a thing noble within its kind. So His words (فأكرمه, "and honoured him") are true of a person who is struck by a benefit without any shame in it, or of one who is made noble, a lord of honour. His words (فأكرمه) belong to the first meaning of honouring, and His words (﴿Then he says: My Lord has honoured me﴾) belong to the second meaning in al-Raghib's words. Know that His words (ونعّمه, "and blessed him") explicitly state that God bestows blessings upon the disbelievers, as a means of awakening them and dealing with them through mercy. What the scholars among the theologians (al-muhaqqiqun) hold is that the disbeliever is blessed in this world. This is the view of al-Maturidi and al-Baqillani. This is among the matters on which al-Ash'ari and al-Maturidi differed, and the difference is verbal.

[p. 331]

The meaning of (نعّمه, "blessed him") is that He placed him in blessing, i.e., in a pleasant life.

The meaning of (فقدر عليه رزقه, "restricted his provision") is that He gave him in a limited measure. From this comes al-taqtir (التقتير, "restriction") with the letter ta' in place of dal. All of this is a metaphor for scarcity, and its opposite is the spreading of provision. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿If God were to spread provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth, but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 27]).

The pronoun in (رزقه, "his provision") may refer to the human being, as an idafah of the verbal noun to its object, or it may refer to (ربه, "his Lord"), as an idafah of the verbal noun to its agent.

Al-ihanah (الإهانة, "humiliation") is treatment with humiliation (al-hawn), which is abasement.

The attribution of (﴿honoured and blessed him﴾ and ﴿restricted his provision﴾) to the Lord, exalted is He, is because honour and blessing come to the human being, or the measure of provision comes to him by causes that are part of God's making and His laws in this worldly life, in what some events coincide with others. There are also causes for the correlation between the occurrence of these meanings and the people who are affected by them, in their opportunities and occasions.

The word (يقول, "says") is used in its literal sense, which is speaking, and a person only speaks out of belief. So the meaning is: "he says, 'My Lord has honoured me,'" believing that, and he says, "My Lord has humiliated me," believing that. For they do not refrain from boasting of blessing, or from complaining about constraint and need. A parallel to this usage of "says" is found in His words, exalted is He: (﴿That is because they said: There is no blame on us regarding the unlettered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]), i.e., they believed that, so they said it and used it as an excuse for themselves among the people of their religion.

The placing of (ربي, "my Lord") before the verb (أكرمني, "honoured me") and the verb (أهانني, "humiliated me"), rather than saying "honoured me my Lord" or "humiliated me my Lord," is for the purpose of strengthening the judgement, i.e., he says that with certainty, without doubt.

The two clauses (فيقول, "then he says") in both places are the responses (jawab) of (أمّا, "as for") in the first and second instances. That is, the human being's utterance of this statement is constant, whenever blessing comes to him and whenever restriction of provision comes to him.

[p. 332]

The imperfect verb is chosen in both responses to convey the repetition and renewal of that saying whenever the content of the two conditions occurs.

The particle (كلّا, "No!") is a rebuke against the human being's saying (﴿My Lord has honoured me﴾) when blessing comes, and his saying (﴿My Lord has humiliated me﴾) when restriction afflicts him. So it is a repudiation of believing that. The basis of the repudiation is both sayings, because each of them proceeds from a false interpretation. That is, the human being's state in this worldly life is not evidence of his rank with God, exalted is He. Rather, God's purpose is known through the ways that God has directed us to through His messengers and His laws. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿Say: Shall We inform you of those who lose most in their deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world, while they think they are doing well in their work﴾ [al-Kahf: 103–104]), up to His words: (﴿So We shall assign them no weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Kahf: 105]), in Surat al-Kahf. Many a man is in blessing in this world, yet he is abhorred by God; and many a dishevelled, dust-covered man, turned away from doors, would, if he swore an oath by God, have it fulfilled by Him.

So the basis of the repudiation is making blessing a sign of God's will to honour the one blessed, and making restriction a sign of His will to humiliate. Its basis is not the occurrence of honour or the occurrence of humiliation. For God humiliates the disbeliever with the punishment of the Hereafter, and if He willed to humiliate him in this world on account of disbelief, He would humiliate all the disbelievers by restricting their provision.

With this it becomes clear that there is no contradiction between affirming God's honouring of the human being by His words (فأكرمه, "and honoured him") and nullifying that by His words (كلّا, "No!"). For the nullification applies to what the human being intended by his words (﴿My Lord has honoured me﴾): that what he received of blessing is a sign of God's approval of him.

So the meaning is that God's dealings with people in this world have secrets and causes that cannot be fully grasped, that people of ignorance are far removed from comprehending its secret through fanciful analogies and reliance on customary familiarities, and that it is better for them to seek realities from their rational proofs, to know God's purpose from His revelation to His messengers, to beware of deviating from proofs away from what they indicate, and not to derive branches without their roots.

As for the people of knowledge, they place things in their proper positions, and they make judgements (yatawassamun) grounded in guidance, and they neither mix up nor stumble about.

[p. 332 continued]

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (ربي, "my Lord") in both places with a fatha on the ya' (ربيَ). The rest read it with sukun (ربي).

The majority read (فقدر عليه, "restricted") with a light dal, and Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read it with a doubled dal.

Nafi' read (أكرمن، وأهانن, "honoured me" and "humiliated me") with a ya' after the nun in pause (waṣl) and without it in stopping (waqf). Ibn Kathir read both with the ya' in both waṣl and waqf. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read both without ya' in both waṣl and waqf. It is written in the Mushaf without a ya' after the two nuns, and there is no conflict between the transmitted reading and the orthography of the Mushaf.

(كلّا, "No!") is a rebuke against this saying, i.e., the testing of God with blessing and with restriction of provision is not caused by God's will to honour the human being, nor by His will to humiliate him. This is a general rebuke, which the Qur'an did not explain in detail, being content with appending to the account of the three nations in their blessing His words: (﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]), after His words: (﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾ [al-Fajr: 13]).

[Page 324]

**﴿Then as for man, when his Lord tests him and honours him and blesses him, he says, "My Lord has honoured me." But when He tests him and restricts his provision, he says, "My Lord has humiliated me." No!﴾** (al-Fajr 89:15–17)

The *fa'* (the particle of consequence) indicates that the speech following it is connected to what precedes it and is necessarily derived from it.

The particle *amma* ("as for") conveys the meaning "whatever may be the case," and this is the basic meaning of the particle and what its usage requires. Its use strengthens the connection of its response to what precedes it and to the *fa'* attached to it. This connection shines out like a flash of lightning, and its brilliance clarifies what was obscure, since the derivation of what follows this *fa'* from what precedes it is hidden. So let us explain it clearly.

The preceding discourse described the enjoyments that the nations mentioned were given by God, who bestowed blessings upon them, while they were heedless of the call of God's messengers, turned away from seeking the pleasure of their Lord, plunged into the evils they had been forbidden, were insolent in their blessings, and were self-admiring in their greatness. Therefore, after mentioning what they were doing and what God requited them with in the form of punishment in this world, the discourse draws a lesson, which is to remind the polytheists that their condition is similar to theirs in luxury, rebellion and insolence, and to warn them of their error. For they had, from their state of luxury and blessing, a semblance upon which they built the delusion that God had made them objects of honour. Thus they reckoned that the Messenger's (ﷺ) warning them of punishment was not true, since it contradicted what they were actually experiencing of blessing. So they imagined that God's treatment of them was a stronger proof of their honour in His sight than what the Messenger (ﷺ) reported, namely that God had commanded them to the opposite of what they were doing. They denied that there could be another world after this one that would contradict it, and they restricted God's giving to what His servants have in this worldly life. This delusion thus led them to deny what they were warned of by way of threat, and the reward in the Hereafter that delights the believers. They confined the recompense of good to wealth and blessing, and confined the recompense of evil to poverty and the restriction of provision.

The Qur'an has repeatedly addressed the refutation of this, as in His saying: ﴿Do they suppose that what We supply them with of wealth and children is [a sign that] We hasten for them good things? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:55–56).

This delusion contains principles upon which the denial of recompense in the Hereafter is built, the denial of a second life, and the assumption that conditions will endure forever.

[Page 325]

So the *fa'* of consequence is linked to the sentence ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ (al-Fajr 89:14), with the generality it contains, which is required by its being a concluding statement (*tadhyil*).

The meaning is: this is the way of your Lord, operating in accordance with His knowledge and wisdom. As for the disbelieving man, he imagines otherwise, since he supposes that the blessing and abundance he receives in this world is an honouring from God to him, and that the narrowness of livelihood he receives is a humiliation with which God has humiliated him.

This delusion entails their thinking that God's acts occur without wisdom. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after some hardship had touched him, he would surely say, "This is my due, and I do not think the Hour will ever come. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him." So We will inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe punishment.﴾ (Fussilat 41:50).

So God informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of the true reality, and alerted them to avoid confusing the fine and lofty proofs, and to avoid making fancy and whim the judge. He reminded them that worldly conditions are fleeting accidents, varying in length and brevity. In all of this is a refutation of the creed of the people of polytheism and their error, which was prevalent among the people of the *Jahiliyya* (the Age of Ignorance). For this reason Nabigha said about the family of Ghassan, who were not polytheists but adhered to Christianity:

*Their assembly is the protection of God, and their religion is upright, so they hope for nothing but the consequences.*
*And they do not reckon good to be without evil after it, nor do they reckon evil to be an inescapable blow.*

God has followed this with rebuke and refutation through His saying "No!" The basis of the rebuke and refutation is both of the two statements, because they both proceed from a false interpretation and a misguided doubt, as you will know when we reach His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then He honoured him and blessed him﴾.

The verse is restricted to the constriction of provision in contrast to blessing, and not to other causes and afflictions, because the majority of the conditions of the polytheists being spoken of were soundness of temperament and strength of bodies. So they did not perish except by killing or old age among them and their relatives. Nabigha said:

*It covers destructions that will not let you wait for old age.*

[Page 326]

Most of the exegetes did not pause to explain the arrangement (*nazm*) of the verse and its connection to what precedes it, except al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya.

This misguided belief is known from the speech of the people of the *Jahiliyya*. Tarafa said:

*Had my Lord willed, I would have been Qays ibn 'Asim,*
*and had my Lord willed, I would have been 'Amr ibn Murthid.*
*So I became possessed of much wealth, and noble sons surrounded me, lords over those who would be lords.*

They made this deception a measure of the ranks of people. They made the people of perfection those with splendid appearances, and they branded the people of poverty and the weak as deficient. For this reason, when the chiefs of Quraysh and of Banu Tamim and Fazara came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while 'Ammar, Bilal, Khabbab, Salim (the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa), Suhayb, and Sabih (the freedman of Usayd), along with other weak believers, were with him, they said to the Prophet: "Drive them away from you, for perhaps if you drive them away, we would follow you." They also said to Abu Talib: "If your nephew were to drive away these slaves and allies, it would be greater in our eyes and more inclined to make us follow him." It was concerning this that God revealed His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾ (al-An'am 6:52), the verse as already mentioned in Surat al-An'am.

So God alerted them to the error of their belief by way of mention of its like among what the nations before them believed, which was the cause that made the punishment pour down upon them. He informed them that the conditions of this world are taken as a basis in considering the recompense for deeds, and that the consistent recompense is the recompense of the Day of Resurrection.

The intended meaning of *al-insan* ("man") is the species, and its definiteness is the definiteness of the species, so it encompasses the individuals of the species. However, this is a customary generality, by which is meant the polytheistic people, since they were the majority among the people being spoken of. This is the predominant usage of the word *insan* in the Qur'an revealed at Mecca, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, man transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ (al-'Alaq 96:6); ﴿Does man suppose that We will not assemble his bones?﴾ (al-Qiyamah 75:3); ﴿We have certainly created man in hardship﴾ and ﴿Does he think that no one has power over him?﴾ (al-Balad 90:4–5), and similar verses. This is supported by His saying: ﴿On that day man will remember, but how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾ (al-Fajr 89:23), and the verse continues.

It has been said that a specific individual was intended: it was said to be 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, or Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira, according to Ibn 'Abbas; and it was said to be Umayya ibn Khalaf, according to Muqatil and al-Kalbi; and it was said to be Ubayy ibn Khalaf, also according to al-Kalbi. But these named individuals are merely examples of misguidance. Ibn 'Atiyya said:

[Page 327]

Since this was predominant among the disbelievers, the reproach in this verse came with the name of the species, since (as is the case) some of the believers may fall into something of this tendency.

Know that among the misguidance of the people of polytheism, and among the temptation of Satan for some ignorant believers, is that there is imagined for them what befalls someone, by attributing it to God's arrangement of the connection of effects to their causes and of caused things to their causes. They therefore place whatever fortunate event befalls one of them into the position of an honour from God toward the one who has encountered the benefits of it, following fancy, self-love, conjecture about the unseen, and presumption against God. And when one of them encounters an event that brings him harm, he imagines it, through his delusions, to be a vengeance from God directed at him, out of pessimism on their part.

Those who claimed that the blessing they received from God was an honouring from God to them are not worthy of God's honour.

And those who imagined that what befell them of scarcity of provision was a humiliation from God to them are not lower in God's sight than those who claimed that God had honoured them with the blessing they are in.

This belief caused the polytheists to be deeply immersed in their polytheism, and diverted their gaze from reflecting on what contradicts it. Satanic whisperings have often become a temptation for some weak believers, short-sighted people, and those ignorant of the true creed, as Ahmad ibn al-Rawandi revealed about the instability of their understanding and the scarcity of their knowledge, in his saying:

*How many a wise person whose paths have baffled him,*
*and a fool, a fool, whom you find provided for!*
*This is what has left minds bewildered,*
*and turned the knowledgeable, expert scholar into a heretic.*

This is what diverted the misguided from seeking the truths from their proofs, and diverted them from reflecting on what brings its possessor the pleasure of God and what brings about His anger. The knowledge of God is vast, and His dispositions are varied, and all of them proceed from wisdom: ﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:255). Harm may come to the servant from several causes, and benefit may come from others. Some of this operates openly in the customary way, and some of it bears the mark of breaking customs. Calamities often come from the directions of benefits, and the one who is granted success is alert to the signs. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened for them the gates of everything until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were then in despair﴾ (al-An'am 6:44). And He said: ﴿We did not send a prophet into any town without seizing its people with adversity and hardship, so that they might humble themselves﴾ (al-A'raf 7:94). ﴿Then We exchanged the bad state for good until they multiplied and said, "Hardship and ease touched our fathers too," so We seized them suddenly while they were unaware﴾ (al-A'raf 7:95). And He said: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested once or twice every year, yet they do not repent nor take heed?﴾ (al-Tawbah 9:126).

[Page 328]

The dispositions of God are similar in nature. Some of them indicate His purpose concerning people, and some of them proceed according to the order of the world that He has decreed. Everything has been decreed and determined by Him, His knowledge preceded it, and He connected its effects to their causes, directly or through an intermediary or intermediaries. The one who has insight takes precaution for himself and his people, does not speak about God what his fancy dictates to him when his proofs do not support it, and entrusts what is unclear to him to the knowledge of God.

The condition of these people reported here is not the condition of the Muslims who are guided by the guidance of the Prophet (ﷺ) and who have insight into the courses of divine dispositions. We may find among the common folk and those who resemble them among the heedless some remnants of the belief of the people of the *Jahiliyya*, in producing the imaginings that their minds dictate to them. So it is incumbent upon them to take admonition from God's admonition in this verse.

Indeed, God may hasten the recompense of good for some of His righteous servants, as He said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ (al-Nahl 16:97). He may also hasten punishment for whomever of His servants He is angry with. He related the words of Noah to his people: ﴿So I said, "Seek forgiveness of your Lord; indeed, He is ever forgiving. He will send down rain upon you in abundance, and provide you with wealth and children"﴾ (Nuh 71:10–12). And He said: ﴿And if they had remained upright on the way, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ (al-Jinn 72:16). This treatment has signs, the most evident of which is that it proceeds contrary to what is customary, as we see in the victory of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the caliphs over great and dominant nations. These are promises from God which He fulfils, or a threat from Him that befalls those who deserve it.

The particle *amma* generally indicates detail, that is, it points to a contrast between two things, whether of essences or of states. For this reason it is repeated in speech. The detail it conveys is not in the sense of clarifying a preceding ambiguity; rather, it is detail, contrast, and balance. This is one of the kinds of detail for which *amma* is used. The connection of the detail to the preceding speech is conveyed by the *fa'* that enters upon *amma*, and its connection to what precedes it is the connection of a derived matter to its source, not a detailed explanation of a general statement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 89, verses 15–16 (part 2 of 2):

[p. 330]

The detail here concerns the states of the ignorant human being. It is explained by his state in ease and comfort, and his state in hardship and distress. The balance between the two states, expressed by the two time clauses in His words (﴿When his Lord tests him and honours him﴾), and in His words (﴿As for when He tests him and restricts his provision﴾), and so on. This detailing is not of the kind that clarifies what is general (mujmal). Rather, it is a distinguishing and separating between two things, or things that resemble each other or become confused.

The particle (أمّا, ʾammā, "as for") has already been discussed at His words, exalted is He: (﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26]), in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-ibtila' (الابتلاء, "testing") means examination, and it occurs through good and through harm, because in both there is a test of the steadfastness of the soul, and of the disposition of forbearance and patience. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35]). By mentioning the testing it becomes clear that God's honouring of him is a honouring that is a test, so it falls into two states: a state that is pleasing (to God) and a state that is not pleasing. Likewise, the restriction of provision is a restriction of testing, which also requires two states. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿That He may test me, whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾ [al-Naml: 40]), and He said: (﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35]). The more common usage is that testing is by harm, but in this verse it is used in both senses.

The meaning is: when his Lord makes what reaches him of blessing, or of restriction, a manifestation of his state in gratitude and ingratitude, and in patience and impatience, he imagines that God has honoured him by that, or humiliated him by this.

On al-ikram (الإكرام, "honouring"), al-Raghib said: "It is that a dignity (karamah) reaches a person, and it is a benefit in which there is no shame or humiliation; and that he makes what reaches him something noble (karim), i.e., honourable. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]), i.e., He made them noble." End of quotation. He means that honouring is applied to giving a dignity, and it is also applied to making a thing noble within its kind. So His words (فأكرمه, "and honoured him") are true of a person who is struck by a benefit without any shame in it, or of one who is made noble, a lord of honour. His words (فأكرمه) belong to the first meaning of honouring, and His words (﴿Then he says: My Lord has honoured me﴾) belong to the second meaning in al-Raghib's words. Know that His words (ونعّمه, "and blessed him") explicitly state that God bestows blessings upon the disbelievers, as a means of awakening them and dealing with them through mercy. What the scholars among the theologians (al-muhaqqiqun) hold is that the disbeliever is blessed in this world. This is the view of al-Maturidi and al-Baqillani. This is among the matters on which al-Ash'ari and al-Maturidi differed, and the difference is verbal.

[p. 331]

The meaning of (نعّمه, "blessed him") is that He placed him in blessing, i.e., in a pleasant life.

The meaning of (فقدر عليه رزقه, "restricted his provision") is that He gave him in a limited measure. From this comes al-taqtir (التقتير, "restriction") with the letter ta' in place of dal. All of this is a metaphor for scarcity, and its opposite is the spreading of provision. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿If God were to spread provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth, but He sends down in measure what He wills﴾ [al-Shura: 27]).

The pronoun in (رزقه, "his provision") may refer to the human being, as an idafah of the verbal noun to its object, or it may refer to (ربه, "his Lord"), as an idafah of the verbal noun to its agent.

Al-ihanah (الإهانة, "humiliation") is treatment with humiliation (al-hawn), which is abasement.

The attribution of (﴿honoured and blessed him﴾ and ﴿restricted his provision﴾) to the Lord, exalted is He, is because honour and blessing come to the human being, or the measure of provision comes to him by causes that are part of God's making and His laws in this worldly life, in what some events coincide with others. There are also causes for the correlation between the occurrence of these meanings and the people who are affected by them, in their opportunities and occasions.

The word (يقول, "says") is used in its literal sense, which is speaking, and a person only speaks out of belief. So the meaning is: "he says, 'My Lord has honoured me,'" believing that, and he says, "My Lord has humiliated me," believing that. For they do not refrain from boasting of blessing, or from complaining about constraint and need. A parallel to this usage of "says" is found in His words, exalted is He: (﴿That is because they said: There is no blame on us regarding the unlettered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]), i.e., they believed that, so they said it and used it as an excuse for themselves among the people of their religion.

The placing of (ربي, "my Lord") before the verb (أكرمني, "honoured me") and the verb (أهانني, "humiliated me"), rather than saying "honoured me my Lord" or "humiliated me my Lord," is for the purpose of strengthening the judgement, i.e., he says that with certainty, without doubt.

The two clauses (فيقول, "then he says") in both places are the responses (jawab) of (أمّا, "as for") in the first and second instances. That is, the human being's utterance of this statement is constant, whenever blessing comes to him and whenever restriction of provision comes to him.

[p. 332]

The imperfect verb is chosen in both responses to convey the repetition and renewal of that saying whenever the content of the two conditions occurs.

The particle (كلّا, "No!") is a rebuke against the human being's saying (﴿My Lord has honoured me﴾) when blessing comes, and his saying (﴿My Lord has humiliated me﴾) when restriction afflicts him. So it is a repudiation of believing that. The basis of the repudiation is both sayings, because each of them proceeds from a false interpretation. That is, the human being's state in this worldly life is not evidence of his rank with God, exalted is He. Rather, God's purpose is known through the ways that God has directed us to through His messengers and His laws. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿Say: Shall We inform you of those who lose most in their deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world, while they think they are doing well in their work﴾ [al-Kahf: 103–104]), up to His words: (﴿So We shall assign them no weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Kahf: 105]), in Surat al-Kahf. Many a man is in blessing in this world, yet he is abhorred by God; and many a dishevelled, dust-covered man, turned away from doors, would, if he swore an oath by God, have it fulfilled by Him.

So the basis of the repudiation is making blessing a sign of God's will to honour the one blessed, and making restriction a sign of His will to humiliate. Its basis is not the occurrence of honour or the occurrence of humiliation. For God humiliates the disbeliever with the punishment of the Hereafter, and if He willed to humiliate him in this world on account of disbelief, He would humiliate all the disbelievers by restricting their provision.

With this it becomes clear that there is no contradiction between affirming God's honouring of the human being by His words (فأكرمه, "and honoured him") and nullifying that by His words (كلّا, "No!"). For the nullification applies to what the human being intended by his words (﴿My Lord has honoured me﴾): that what he received of blessing is a sign of God's approval of him.

So the meaning is that God's dealings with people in this world have secrets and causes that cannot be fully grasped, that people of ignorance are far removed from comprehending its secret through fanciful analogies and reliance on customary familiarities, and that it is better for them to seek realities from their rational proofs, to know God's purpose from His revelation to His messengers, to beware of deviating from proofs away from what they indicate, and not to derive branches without their roots.

As for the people of knowledge, they place things in their proper positions, and they make judgements (yatawassamun) grounded in guidance, and they neither mix up nor stumble about.

[p. 332 continued]

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (ربي, "my Lord") in both places with a fatha on the ya' (ربيَ). The rest read it with sukun (ربي).

The majority read (فقدر عليه, "restricted") with a light dal, and Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read it with a doubled dal.

Nafi' read (أكرمن، وأهانن, "honoured me" and "humiliated me") with a ya' after the nun in pause (waṣl) and without it in stopping (waqf). Ibn Kathir read both with the ya' in both waṣl and waqf. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read both without ya' in both waṣl and waqf. It is written in the Mushaf without a ya' after the two nuns, and there is no conflict between the transmitted reading and the orthography of the Mushaf.

(كلّا, "No!") is a rebuke against this saying, i.e., the testing of God with blessing and with restriction of provision is not caused by God's will to honour the human being, nor by His will to humiliate him. This is a general rebuke, which the Qur'an did not explain in detail, being content with appending to the account of the three nations in their blessing His words: (﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr: 14]), after His words: (﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾ [al-Fajr: 13]).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 89, verses 17–20:

﴿Nay, but you do not honour the orphan﴾ ﴿nor urge one another to feed the needy﴾ ﴿and you devour the inheritance greedily﴾ ﴿and you love wealth with excessive love﴾.

(Bal) is a transitional *idrab* (a turn from one subject to another). The connection between the subject being left and the subject being moved to is a connection of contrast with the content of (﴿So He honours him and bestows favours upon him﴾ [al-Fajr: 15]). This is because they supposed that the blessing of their wealth and the ease of their living was an honour from God to them. God therefore alerted them that, if God honoured them, they did not honour His servants, out of stinginess with the blessing. They deprived the needy of the surplus of their wealth, and they sought to increase the wealth they did not need. This refutes their boasting of generosity and giving.

The clause (﴿you do not honour the orphan﴾) is a resumption (*istinaf*), as the *idrab* requires. It is either the resumption of a new statement or an interjection (*i'tiradh*) between (*kalla*, "no!") and its sister, as will come. Honouring the orphan means meeting his need and treating him well, because he is the object of need through the loss of his guardian, and because of their seizing the wealth that fathers leave for their young children. In the pre-Islamic period, wealth was passed around among the heads of households.

Kindness (*al-birr*) is included, because the orphan is the object of a broken heart through his sense of losing the one on whom he relied.

The orphan (*al-yatim*) is the young boy whose father has died; this was discussed in surah al-Nisa. The definite article here is for the category: "you do not honour orphans." The same applies to the definite article in "the needy" (*al-miskin*).

The negation of urging to feed the needy is a negation of feeding them by a stronger argument (*bi-tariq al-awla*). This is the indication of the implication of the address (*dalalat fahwa al-khitab*): that is, because they are indifferent to the needy, they do not benefit them even by intercession, let alone benefit them by giving from their wealth.

The phrase (*tha'am*, "food") may be a noun meaning "what is eaten," with the sense: "and you do not urge one another to give the food of the needy." Then its idafa to "the needy" is in the sense of the *lam* of entitlement. It may also be a verbal noun of *atham* (to feed), meaning: "and you do not urge one another to feed the needy from the rich." Then its idafa to "the needy" is the idafa of a verbal noun to its object.

The *miskin* is the poor person. This was discussed in surah al-Bara'a.

There is *ihtibak* in the verse, because when their honouring of the orphan was negated and paired with the negation of urging the feeding of the needy, it is understood that they do not urge the honouring of their orphans, that is, they do not urge the guardians of orphans to do so. It is also understood that they do not feed the needy from their wealth.

It is possible that urging to food is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for feeding. This is because whoever urges the doing of something desires to engage in it, and when he is able to do it, he does it. From this is the saying of God the Exalted: (﴿and they enjoined one another to truth and enjoined one another to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3]), meaning: they acted upon the truth and were patient, and they enjoined both upon one another.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read (﴿you do not honour﴾, ﴿you do not urge﴾, ﴿you devour﴾, ﴿you love﴾) with the second-person *ta'* (*bi-l-muthannat al-fawqiyya*), in the form of *iltifat* (a shift) from the third person in His saying: (﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him﴾ [al-Fajr: 15]) and the verses that follow, for the purpose of confronting them with reproach. Confrontation is more forceful for this than the third person. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read them with the *ya'* below (*bi-l-muthanna al-tahtiyya*), in the third person, in order to inform the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims of this, exposing their hidden intentions, in the manner of His saying: (﴿He says, "I have squandered wealth in abundance."﴾ [al-Balad: 6]) (﴿Does he think that no one sees him?﴾ [al-Balad: 7]).

The majority read (*wa-la tahuddunna*, "and you do not urge") with a *damma* on the *ha'* as the present tense of *hadda*. 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, and Khalaf read (*tahaddun*) with a *fatha* on the *ha'* and an alif after it, the present tense of *haddah* (urging one another), whose original form is (*tatahaddun*). One of the two *ta'*s was deleted for lightness. The meaning is: you collude with one another in abandoning the urging to feed.

*Al-turath* is the inherited wealth, that is, the wealth that a man leaves for his heir after his death. Its original form is *wurath*, with a *waw* at the beginning, in the pattern *fu'al*, from the root *wa-ra-tha* (to inherit), in the sense of the passive participle, like *al-diqaq* and *al-hutam*. Its *waw* was changed to *ta'* contrary to analogy, as they did in *tujah*, *tukhamah*, *tuhmah*, *tuqah*, and similar words.

﴿Nay, but you do not honour the orphan﴾ ﴿nor urge one another to feed the needy﴾ ﴿and you devour the inheritance greedily﴾ ﴿and you love wealth with excessive love﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 89, verse 21–26 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 335]
(﴿Nay!﴾).
It is a rebuke and a deterrent against the deeds mentioned before it: their not honouring the orphan, their not urging one another to feed the needy, their devouring inheritance (al-turath), which is the wealth of others, and their loving wealth with an abundant love.
* * *
(﴿When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded to powder, and your Lord comes, and the angels in rows, row upon row. And on that Day Hell is brought near; on that Day man will remember, but how will remembrance benefit him?﴾ ﴿He will say: "Oh, would that I had sent forth for my life!"﴾ ﴿On that Day none will punish as He punishes,﴾ ﴿nor will anyone bind as He binds.﴾).

This is a resumptive, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), shifting from the threat of worldly punishment mentioned in His saying: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad?﴾ [al-Fajr: 6] and the verses that follow, to the warning of punishment in the Hereafter. Even if they made light of what befell the nations before them, or were given respite so that worldly punishment was delayed for them, there is a punishment from which they cannot escape awaiting them on the Day of Resurrection, when they will be compelled to remember, but remembrance will not benefit them, and they will regret, but it will be too late for regret.

The summary of the preceding speech is that the disbelieving man is deluded: he attributes events to other than their causes, imagines them otherwise than they are, and does not heed the call of the Messengers, so he remains in blindness throughout his life. He has been rebuked for this with an emphatic rebuke.

Following their rebuke is a warning that a day will come for them in which they will awaken from their heedlessness, when awakening will no longer benefit them.

The purpose of this speech is His saying: (﴿On that Day none will punish as He punishes﴾) and His saying: (﴿O soul at peace﴾ [al-Fajr: 27]). As for what precedes, from His saying ﴿When the earth is pounded﴾ to His saying ﴿On that Day Hell is brought near﴾, it is a preparation and a stirring of anticipation for hearing what follows, and an amplification of the greatness of that Day, which is defined by the clause "the earth is pounded" and the clauses after it. It is defined by the signs of its arrival and by the terror of punishment that occurs in it.

[p. 336]
Al-dakk means smashing and breaking.

By "the earth" is meant the sphere on which people live. Its pounding is its smashing and the scattering of its parts, arising from the corruption of the present order upon which it exists, and this is by what God brings about in it of earthquakes, as in His saying: (﴿When the earth is shaken with its shaking﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1]), and so on.

(Dakkan dakkan) may have the first of them in the accusative as an absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) emphasizing its verb. Perhaps its emphasis here is because this verse is the first verse in which the pounding of the mountains is mentioned, and since it is a matter contrary to habit, the context required affirming its occurrence in reality, without metaphor or exaggeration. So it is emphasized twice here, and it was not emphasized in its counterpart in His saying: (﴿and they are pounded with one pounding﴾ [al-Haqqah: 14]) in Surat al-Haqqah. Thus the first "dakkan" is intended to remove the possibility of metaphor from "dukkatā" (were pounded), i.e., it is a real pounding. The second "dakkan," in the accusative, is a lexical emphasis (tawkid lafzi) of the first "dakkan," to increase the certainty of the intended literal meaning of pounding, because the pounding of the great earth is a wondrous matter; due to its strangeness, affirming it required increased certainty of its literal meaning.

Al-Radi followed this view, saying: "An exception to the prohibition of emphasizing indefinite nouns (i.e., lexical emphasis) is one thing: it is permissible to emphasize them when the indefinite noun is a predicate and not the subject, as in his saying ﷺ: «Her marriage is void, void, void». Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: (﴿The earth is pounded, pounded to powder﴾), which is like: 'Daraba daraba Zayd'." End of quotation.

This agrees with what is said in describing the pounding of the earth in Surat al-Haqqah with His saying, exalted is He: (﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and pounded with one pounding﴾ [al-Haqqah: 14]), and it removes any contradiction between this and what is in Surat al-Haqqah.

It is also possible that the two verbal nouns together, in the sense of a single noun in the accusative, function as an absolute object specifying the type (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq al-mubayyin lil-naw'). Its meaning is that it is a pounding in which one part follows another, as you say: "I read the book chapter by chapter" (babaan babaan). It is in this sense that the author of al-Kashshaf and most commentators after him explained it, while some commentators remained silent about its explanation. Al-Tibi said: "Ibn al-Hajib said: perhaps he said it in his Amali on the Al-Muqaddimah al-Kafiyah — my copy of it has a lacuna, and I know no other in Tunis, and this statement is not found in Idah al-Mufassal — 'I explained its reckoning to him bab by bab,' i.e., in detail. The Arabs repeat a thing twice, thereby covering the detail of its kind with respect to the meaning indicated by the repeated word. [p. 339]

He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When the shackles are upon their necks and the chains, they will be dragged through the boiling water﴾ [Ghafir: 71], and so on, to the end of the verse.

It may also be for definition or specification, if God places an inspiration in their hearts by which they know that they are at peace.

Tranquility has been explained as certainty of God's existence and oneness, and as certainty in God's promise, and as sincerity in action. Undoubtedly, all of these are among the constituents of the intended tranquility, so its totality is meant and its parts are intended as well. It has also been explained as their being given the glad tidings of Paradise, that is, before their call, and then they were called to enter Paradise.

Return admits both literal and metaphorical meanings, as you know from the earlier aspects of the meaning of the verse.

*Al-radiyyah* is the one who is pleased with what she has been given of honour. It is a *kinaya* (metonymy) for giving her everything she aspires to.

[p. 344]

Surat al-Balad

This surah is called in the translation from Sahih al-Bukhari "Surat La Uqsimu" ("Surah I Swear Not"), and in the Mushafs and books of tafsir it is called "Surat al-Balad" ("the City"). The name either quotes the word at its beginning, for the well-known city intended, which is Makkah.

It is Meccan. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi related a consensus on this, and most exegetes limited themselves to it. Ibn 'Atiyyah related from some people that it is Medinan. Perhaps this is the view of those who explained His saying ﴿and you are a resident of this city﴾ [90:2] to mean that he was given permission to fight on the Day of Conquest, taking "wa anta hill" to mean "and you are now permitted." This goes back to what al-Qurtubi related from al-Suddi and Abu Salih, attributed to Ibn Abbas. Al-Kashshaf pointed to refuting this by noting that the surah was revealed in Makkah by consensus, but using this to refute it is question-begging. The proper refutation is that in His saying ﴿Does he think that no one has power over him?﴾ [90:5] up to ﴿But he has not broken through the steep ascent﴾ [90:11], there are third-person pronouns that must refer back to "man" in ﴿We have created man in hardship﴾ [90:4]; otherwise the pronouns would lack an antecedent. Al-Itqan related a view that it is Medinan, except for the first four verses.

It is counted as the thirty-fifth surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat Qaf and before Surat al-Tariq. Its number of verses is twenty.

* * *

It contains, among its themes: praise of Makkah, of the Prophet's ﷺ residence there, and of the blessing God placed in it and upon its people. It praises the Prophet's ﷺ forefathers among its inhabitants, who were prophets, such as Ibrahim and Isma'il, or followers of the *hanifiyyah* (the pure monotheistic faith), such as 'Adnan and Mudar, as will come. It moves to censure the conduct of the people of polytheism and their denial of resurrection, the excessive boasting they were upon, and their neglect of thanking God for the blessings of the senses, the blessing of speech, the blessing of reason, and the blessing of guidance, so they did not give thanks for these by spending in the paths of good, and what they neglected of the qualities and morals of faith. It also contains a warning to the disbelievers and good tidings to the certain believers.

[p. 341]

When the discussion had fully covered what the context required of threat, warning, and admonition, the Qur'an closed the passage with good tidings for the believers who took heed through the Qur'an and followed its guidance. This follows the Qur'an's habit of pairing warning with good tidings and the reverse, since this increases people's eagerness to do good and their fear of wrongdoing.

The connection of this verse with the verses before it, both in recitation and in the arrangement of the Mushaf, rests on the principle that it was revealed in one sequence with the verses preceding it. This requires that the speech be said in the Hereafter, so it may be said on the Day of Recompense. It is then the quoted speech of an omitted verb of saying, which is the answer to *idha* ("when") in ﴿When the earth is crushed﴾ and what lies between them is a digression and a parenthetical interjection.

This is a statement issued on the Day of Resurrection, either from the holy side of God Most High's speech or from the speech of the angels. If it is from God's speech, then His saying "to your Lord" is an explicit noun in place of a pronoun (*izhar fi maqam al-idmar*), as shown by the *fa* of "enter among My servants" that follows it. The point of this explicit mention is what the title "Lord" carries of closeness and special care, and what its attribution to the pronoun of the addressed soul carries of honour for her.

If it is from the speech of the angels, then the word "your Lord" follows the expected form, and the conjunction in "enter among My servants" is a conjunction of instruction (*'atf talqin*) issuing from God's speech, confirming the angels' words "return to your Lord."

Returning to God is a metaphor (*majaz*) for being in the bliss of Paradise, which is the abode of honour with God, like the abode of a host. He says: ﴿In a seat of truth, with a Sovereign, Omnipotent﴾ [54:55]. Paradise is thus likened to a dwelling for the addressed soul, because she deserved it through God's promise for her righteous deeds, as though she had been estranged from it in the world, so she is told: return to it. This return is specific, not a general settling in the Hereafter.

It is also possible that the verse is a fresh, independent resumption, in keeping with the mention of the punishment of the polytheistic human. Then it is an address from God to the souls of the believers who are at peace.

The imperative "return to your Lord" is intended to be restricted by the two states that follow it, namely ﴿well-pleased and well-pleasing﴾. This is the use of the imperative to express a promise. The return is also metaphorical. The pronoun in "among My servants" and "My Paradise" is an *iltifat* (a shift from third person to first person).

Some exegetes said that the verse was revealed about a particular person. From al-Dahhak: it was revealed about Uthman ibn Affan when he gave the well of Rumah in charity. From Buraydah: it was revealed about Hamza when he was killed. It was also said that it was revealed about Khubayb ibn Adi when the people of Makkah crucified him. These views imply that this verse is

[p. 342]

Medinan. The consensus, however, is that the surah is Meccan, except for what al-Dani related from some scholars, that it is Medinan. On that view, it is separate from what precedes it, and it was written here by a special *tawqif* (divine instruction), or it was revealed after what precedes it for the sake of connection.
